title: Newcastle players see Jaissle's angry side - can they respond?
description: Newcastle United head coach Matthias Jaissle was forthright in the away dressing room at Elland Road on Monday night following a chastening 4-1 defeat against Leeds United.
fullText:
Newcastle United players had previously experienced an unhappy Matthias Jaissle in training in the opening weeks of his reign.

But the head coach was especially forthright in the away dressing room at Elland Road on Monday.

It was a night the visitors suffered a chastening 4-1 defeat against Leeds United.

"There was all clarity in the room that the learning curve needs to be really fast," Jaissle said a few days on.

Even during the course of a previous five-game unbeaten run, there was a recognition within the club that this was "always going to be a work in progress" following a summer of huge change.

Newcastle have gone from having one of the most experienced starting line-ups in the Premier League last season to the second-youngest this time around.

Yet the manner of Newcastle's first loss of the campaign still came as a jolt.

It already feels like much will be learned from how Jaissle's team respond against in-form Hull City on Saturday.

"If you're tougher in the duels, if you're more aggressive, if you're more sharp and hungry to collect the second balls, then it will be automatically a huge step already," he said.

"That means that you're more dominant, that you have more possession, and then that leads also to the fact that you threaten the opposition much more.

"So they will be the elements where we will focus on and there will be a reaction."

Jaissle was parachuted into the hot seat just three weeks before the start of the season after predecessor Eddie Howe stepped down.

He is still adapting to the Premier League and injuries to, among others, Dan Burn, Joelinton, Anthony Elanga and William Osula have hardly helped in that regard.

That being said, no team have faced more shots (76) in the opening weeks of the season in the top flight, while at the other end Newcastle have been averaging little more than three efforts on target per game in the league.

The visitors struggled to gain a foothold against an aggressive Leeds side, even before influential midfielder Nico Gonzalez went off with a concussion in the 19th minute.

Vertical football is Jaissle's trademark, in an effort to "stress" the opposition, but too often Newcastle's main tactic appeared to be punting the ball forward for Yoane Wissa and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to chase hopefully at Elland Road.

Leeds' three towering centre-backs outnumbered the pair and Newcastle were also swarmed in midfield after Jaissle stuck with his preferred two-man pivot.

However exposed Jaissle's system was, though, that does not excuse those on the field failing to do the basics from the off against one of the most physical sides in the league.

Meek Newcastle lost 56% of their duels in the first half against Leeds and defenders Malick Thiaw and Sven Botman were bullied by Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who scored twice.

A warning had previously been sounded when Newcastle failed to match Bournemouth's intensity and found themselves 2-0 down after just 35 minutes earlier this month.

Jaissle's team showed admirable grit and spirit to come back and draw that game at St James' Park, but a similar response was never on the cards in West Yorkshire.

No wonder one or two Newcastle players threw out their palms apologetically as they trudged over to the away end at full-time.

Jaissle repeatedly stressed his "fundamentals" - being physical, intense and competitive in duels - were "non-negotiable" and how his players needed to take losing a duel personally.

He spent the bus journey home digging into the detail behind the defeat with his analysts.

However, just as Jaissle has not allowed himself to get too high following positive results, he has not tended to emotionally rip up the foundations after a setback, either, as former Red Bull Salzburg midfielder Zlatko Junuzovic explained.

"They analysed the situation and, where necessary, made one or two adjustments, but nothing drastic," he said of his approach to defeats during their time in Austria.

"I think he's still in a phase of figuring things out [at Newcastle], where he has to see for himself which players fit his system and which ones don't."

Jaissle, 38, may still be a relatively young manager but he has experience to fall back on in that regard.

It was a different level, a different sort of capitulation and a different squad, but Jaissle also suffered a bruising away defeat at a similar point of his reign at Al-Ahli after the Saudi Pro League side were hammered 5-1 by Al-Fateh in 2023.

Could that difficult night in Leeds prove a similarly valuable learning experience or will this campaign be characterised by further ups and downs?

"We don't search for excuses, even with a young squad," Jaissle said. "We need to learn fast."

Saint-Maximin on speaking out after his children were racially abused

title: Abhishek hits fastest century in full-member T20s
description: Abhishek Sharma hits a 30-ball century - the fastest in a T20 international between two full-member nations - in India's third T20 against Afghanistan.
fullText:
India 221-7 (20 overs): Abhishek 108 (34), Samson 50 (35); Omarzai 2-27

Afghanistan 94 (14.1 overs): Zadran 25 (16); Bishnoi 3-26

Abhishek Sharma hit a 30-ball century - the fastest in a T20 international between two full-member nations - in India's 127-run victory in the third T20 against Afghanistan in Delhi.

Opener Abhishek, who was knocked off the top of the T20 batting rankings in July, continued to make 108 from 34 balls, hitting nine fours and 11 sixes in India's 221-7.

The 26-year-old reached three figures in the ninth over - at that stage India were 132-0 - having scored a remarkable 96 of his 100 runs in boundaries.

The only exceptions were the single to get to his hundred, another in the previous over and a two in the third.

It was Abhishek's third T20 international ton and the 10th of his entire T20 career.

And while it beat the previous fastest century for a full-member nation - a 33-ball effort by New Zealand's Finn Allen against South Africa at this year's T20 World Cup - it was not even Abhishek's quickest in the format.

The thrilling left-hander hit a 28-ball ton for Punjab against Meghalaya in Indian domestic cricket in 2024.

Against Afghanistan, he dominated Afghanistan's pace bowlers with his pull shot and powered the spinners down the ground.

He helped India take 100 from the powerplay but, after he was caught behind off the bowling of Rashid Khan, the hosts added 79 in the remaining 10.1 overs.

Afghanistan collapsed to 94 in response, giving the hosts a 3-0 series clean sweep.

Notifications, social media and more with BBC Sport

title: Saudi Arabia dropped from World Rally Championship
description: The final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship will be held in Italy instead of Saudi Arabia because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.
fullText:
The final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship (WRC) will be held in Italy instead of Saudi Arabia because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia had been set to host the 14th and final rally of the season from 11-14 November.

The championship has now been shortened to 13 rounds and will conclude with the Rally Italia in Sardinia from 1-4 October.

Rally Saudi Arabia in Jeddah, which joined the WRC calendar in 2025, will still take place on the planned dates but as part of the Middle East Rally Championship.

The FIA, the global governing body for motor sports, said Saudi Arabia "remained ready to host the event safely" but the decision was due to "ongoing uncertainty in the region and its effect on logistical arrangements".

White, Netherlands, Evans and sport's other great runners-up

Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca

In a statement, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "We have worked closely with our partners to explore every possible route that would allow Rally Saudi Arabia to take place as planned.

"These are never easy decisions, particularly after the significant work undertaken by everyone involved in preparing for the event.

"While the WRC element of the event will not take place this year, our confidence in the organisers and in the long-term future of the rally remains unchanged."

Great Britain's Elfyn Evans sits at the top of the WRC standings before the final round, 17 points clear of Finland's Sami Pajari, and is the favourite to take the title with a maximum of 35 points up for grabs across the final round.

The Welshman has finished runner-up in the championship five times, and is looking to join former British winners Colin McRae and Richard Burns in winning the title.

Numerous conflicts are ongoing in the Middle East, including the Israel-Gaza war, with Israel and the United States at war with Iran and Saudi Arabia battling Houthi rebels in Yemen.

The WRC is not the first sporting event to avoid the region, with the FIA cancelling Formula One Grand Prix races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia in April.

The Bahrain race has since been relocated to Malaysia - to be staged in early October - with races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi later in the season are scheduled to go ahead as planned.

In February, tennis players, staff and media were left stranded in Dubai following missile strikes on the United Arab Emirates while in March, an ATP Challenger event in the country was disrupted by drone strikes. The sport's governing bodies are reportedly considering replacement hosts for events in the region for the 2027 season.

On Wednesday, English golfer Matt Fitzpatrick said he is not "100% comfortable" with prospect of travelling to Dubai for his DP World Tour Championship title defence in November.

title: The big questions for Tuchel's first England squad since World Cup
description: Before Thomas Tuchel names his first squad since the World Cup on Friday, BBC Sport looks at the big questions facing the England boss.
fullText:
Sixty-five days after England's semi-final defeat by Argentina, Thomas Tuchel will name his first squad since the World Cup on Friday.

While the tournament ultimately ended with a spectacular 6-4 win over France in the bronze-medal match, the Three Lions left the United States with a long list of what ifs.

Now, with four games in the space of 11 days coming up during the extended international break, fans will get a glimpse of what Tuchel's next England side might look like.

Could players like Trent Alexander-Arnold be recalled? Will others like Alex Scott make their debut? And how might we expect them to play?

BBC Sport senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel, journalist Jess Anderson and BBC Radio 5 Live's John Murray go through the big questions facing Tuchel.

Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcoming Nations League internationals, though it remains to be seen whether they make the final cut.

Liverpool winger Ngumoha was part of a contingent of young players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Palm Beach.

He was unexpectedly handed his debut in the warm-up game against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo.

But the 18-year-old is yet to be picked in a full senior England squad - although he is in with a chance of being selected by Tuchel for the forthcoming games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Hall's World Cup omission raised eyebrows given England entered the tournament without a natural left-back.

Before naming his full squad on Friday, Tuchel is required to submit a preliminary squad of players from which he will name his final party.

It is understood Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly and Everton pair Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Jarrad Branthwaite are also among the names selected in Tuchel's extended list.

Attacking duo Cole Palmer and Phil Foden are on there too, after being two of the biggest omissions from Tuchel's squad for the World Cup.

That decision was deemed a mistake from certain circles, given they are two of English football's most creative players.

Meanwhile, Tuchel is expected to omit Jordan Henderson, Dean Henderson and John Stones because of injury.

Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico

FA to canvass England players in World Cup review

Jess Anderson: One of the most talked-about issues surrounding England is who they turn to in the absence of captain and star striker Harry Kane. At the World Cup, Tuchel simply did not turn to anyone. Kane started all seven of England's matches up to the semi-final and was substituted only twice - both times late on with the game already won.

Kane was rested for the bronze-medal match, with Ivan Toney the preferred option, although the Al-Ahli striker did not score in the 6-4 win over France. Toney will not be an option this international break as he has since been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear in court later this month.

Ollie Watkins' shock summer move to Saudi Arabia puts his England future into question, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin is the man in form with four goals in four games for Leeds United.

This could be the moment for Tuchel to start to further integrate Liam Delap, who is improving at new club Nottingham Forest and has yet to make a senior England appearance. He scored his first goal for Forest in last weekend's win at Aston Villa.

John Murray: In the immediate aftermath of the semi-final in Atlanta, Tuchel and the players spoke of being too passive. At the squad announcement it will be interesting to hear what conclusions Tuchel has reached on why that was the case, and how they came to surrender the initiative to Argentina from 1-0 up with just over half an hour to play.

Head of the queue for a recall is Cole Palmer, who seems to have recaptured the form he was missing last season, which resulted in his omission from the World Cup squad.

What England fans will want to see against Spain at Wembley, is Palmer and his like taking the initiative and imposing themselves on their opponents in a way that was so lacking in the latter stages against Argentina in July.

John Murray: Happy or not, that's what they've got - but this has to be better than another group of qualifiers such as the one they had for the World Cup, against teams way below them in the world rankings.

In those matches last autumn England played some of the best football they have so far produced under Tuchel.

But, while that helped establish patterns of play and build confidence, you never really know until you face the best. That clearly will be the case from the outset in the Nations League, with this opening match against the new world champions.

These matches will also provide preparation for the next Euros in 2028 when, assuming they qualify, England will be playing opponents like this at Wembley. And, lest you forget, this tournament does provide an opportunity to win a trophy which would be the best possible way for Tuchel and his team to step on from their third place at the World Cup.

Sami Mokbel: This will be a key theme to watch over the next three weeks. The spirit was high in the England camp during the World Cup - as evidenced by their brilliant victory against Mexico in the last 16 with 10 men.

But the devastating semi-final defeat by Argentina, and questions over England's approach as a 1-0 lead became a 2-1 loss late on, led to some form of an inquest in the England camp into what was to blame.

Away from the height of those emotions in July, the Football Association is completing a review into England's World Cup campaign. The FA has been keen to stress that this assessment is a standard process, rather than an indication of wider concern or alarm about England's third-place finish.

Indeed, key figures at the FA view the tournament in which England achieved their best finish since 1966 as a success, and the organisation has already backed Tuchel before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign.

Tuchel and members of his backroom team gave their contributions to the review at St George's Park in late August. England players' opinions are also being gathered before a report is presented to senior bosses at the FA.

The ongoing review will also look into the impact of the team's permanent Kansas City base during the tournament. After every game, they returned to Kansas City - and the effects of the travelling will be analysed.

The content of the review won't be made public, but the next three weeks will give an indication of whether the camp is still as together as that night at the Azteca.

'Unplayable' & 'almost perfect' - Calvert-Lewin set for England recall?

Why will September international break last three weeks?

Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico

title: 'Built differently' - Hodgkinson reveals hamstring abnormality
description: Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says she is "built differently" after an MRI scan uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring.
fullText:
Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says an MRI scan has uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring.

Following a suspected tear last year, Hodgkinson had a scan which revealed she has a "split" hamstring, giving her two tendons instead of one.

The 24-year-old is still learning how to manage the anomaly, which allows her to continue running when one of the tendons is torn but may also make her more susceptible to breakdowns.

Following her second-place finish to Swiss Audrey Werro in the 800m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest in September, Hodgkinson announced she had sustained another hamstring tear at the European Championships in Birmingham a few weeks earlier.

"My body is quite literally built differently," said Hodgkinson. "Where most people have one tendon, mine is split - I have two - and we're trying to figure out if it's a strength or a weakness.

"So when one of them tore, I still had another one because it's split. In Birmingham, it didn't affect me during the race, but I could feel something wasn't quite right.

"It's a weird one. You can still run on them. I haven't missed any training the last three weeks. But I've just had to alter my approach. I've had to take my foot off the speed [training], because that's when it's most risky."

The 'F1 of athletics'? Athlos set for London debut

Hodgkinson second to Werro after hamstring tear

Hodgkinson has endured two injury-plagued seasons since winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, waiting for more than a year to race again after suffering a hamstring injury the following February.

Impressing on her return in August 2025 with back-to-back Diamond League wins, she went on to set a new indoor 800m world record in February 2026 before winning gold at the World Indoor Championships a month later.

However, she has been unable to replicate that form outdoors, suffering three defeats by Werro, including losing her European crown to the 22-year-old.

Hodgkinson has since said she suffered a freak injury while jogging along a canal during a warm-down session, sustaining cuts to both knees and whiplash-like jarring in her back which have made the past few months a "battle".

But, while acknowledging that the fall could have contributed to her injury at the European Championships - which ruled her out of Diamond League meets in Zurich and Brussels - she stressed she is not making excuses.

"Part of me wants to talk about it and then part of me doesn't, because I feel like my words get twisted or people are like 'oh, she's making excuses'," Hodgkinson said.

"Going into the Europeans, I thought I was in the best shape ever. But when I fell over, that kind of messed me up way more than I thought it did. I think that's what contributed to my hamstring, because I couldn't really use my quad for a while."

Speaking after her defeat by Werro at the Ultimate Championship, Hodgkinson described 2026 as "frustrating" but remained optimistic: "Overall, I'm finishing second in the world and I can't really be too hard on myself for that."

Hodgkinson will end her 2026 season in London at the all-female Athlos event, launched by Reddit founder Alexis Ohanian, on Friday.

London misses out to Nairobi in World Athletics bid

Sweeney ad a barrier for girls in sport - Hunt

Brands v country - Kerr ramps up kit battle after latest victory

title: This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
description: Queensland's Fitzroy River has been selected for the 2032 Games, despite concerns over the course - and its inhabitants.
fullText:
The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.

Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.

"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.

But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.

While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.

And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.

"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.

Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.

"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.

"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."

The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.

But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.

"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.

"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."

Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.

But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.

Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".

Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.

On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.

There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.

The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."

In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.

The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.

But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.

The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.

They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.

The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.

"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.

"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."

Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".

Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.

The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.

"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.

Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".

The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water.

Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games.

"For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School.

"The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally."

Brisbane to build 63,000-seater stadium for 2032 Games

title: Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards
description:
Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes
Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery.
A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up by Facebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes

Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery.

A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up by Facebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.

The board said Meta’s safeguards were “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes.

“From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair.

“These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.”

In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.”

The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements.

Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label.

In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes.

“The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said.

The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content.

In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms.

The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do.

The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.

title: Buckingham Palace broke its own golden rule over Princess Diana claims
description:
Britain's royal family has taken the unusual step of publicly challenging claims made by Princess Diana's brother, Earl Spencer, in his upcoming memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, excerpts of which were published by Britain's Daily Mail, 
Departing from the monarchy's traditional "never complain, never explain" approach, Buckingham Palace responded Wednesday to Spencer’s recollection of phone calls between himself and King Charles in the wake of Diana's death in 1997
According to Spencer, Charles “sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner” in a call immediately following her passing.
“He let me know he had informed William and Harry of their mother’s death, first thing that morning, in their bedrooms at Balmoral. It all sounded strangely matter-of-fact, given the enormity of the disaster,” Spencer writes in the book. “Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.”

fullText:
Britain's royal family has taken the unusual step of publicly challenging claims made by Princess Diana's brother, Earl Spencer, in his upcoming memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, excerpts of which were published by Britain's Daily Mail,

Departing from the monarchy's traditional "never complain, never explain" approach, Buckingham Palace responded Wednesday to Spencer's recollection of phone calls between himself and King Charles in the wake of Diana's death in 1997

According to Spencer, Charles "sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner" in a call immediately following her passing.

"He let me know he had informed William and Harry of their mother's death, first thing that morning, in their bedrooms at Balmoral. It all sounded strangely matter-of-fact, given the enormity of the disaster," Spencer writes in the book. "Looking back now, I suspect the prince's first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not."

Spencer also recalled another conversation he had with Charles about Diana's funeral arrangements. Spencer had objected to the idea of William and Harry, then 15 and 12, walking behind their mother's coffin at her funeral.

"He unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death," Spencer recalls in the book. "'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough.'"

While the palace didn't directly address whether the comment was made, the statement questioned the reliability of Spencer's recollection, saying, "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss."

The statement echoes the palace's reaction to claims made by Harry and Meghan Markle during their 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey that an unnamed royal had made a remark about their son's skin color before he was born and that the monarchy failed to help a suicidal Meghan. A response issued on behalf of Queen Elizabeth II at that time said that "recollections may vary."

Royal correspondents described Wednesday's statement as highly unusual. Sky News's Laura Bundock called it "a really remarkable intervention" and a "very robust response" that is "beyond punchy." Bundock added that the royal family "simply cannot stay silent."

The BBC's former royal correspondent Jennie Bond described the statement as "'recollections may vary' with bells on. [It] suggests they are going to hit back on this," she said, adding, "It's a right mess."

Rather than a formal palace rule, the "never complain, never explain" phrase is an unofficial code of conduct, often credited to the Victorian-era British prime minister Benjamin Disraeli. The saying was later linked to Elizabeth II's mother and subsequently became a mantra that Elizabeth herself followed. Britain's former monarch almost never responded to criticism, political disputes or reports about her family during her 70-year reign.

Charles has also stuck to the same approach and has not responded to Harry's 2023 memoir Spare, despite numerous allegations about Charles, Queen Camilla and William. Similarly, the palace declined to comment on Tom Bower's book Rebel Prince and Omid Scobie's 2023 book Endgame.

Harry commented on the phrase during a 2023 interview with CBS's 60 Minutes, claiming the reality was more complicated.

"The family motto is 'never complain, never explain,' but it's just a motto," he said. "[Buckingham Palace] will feed or have a conversation with a correspondent, and that correspondent will literally be spoon-fed information and write the story, and at the bottom of it, they will say they have reached out to Buckingham Palace for comment. But the whole story is Buckingham Palace commenting."

Katie Nicholl, a Vanity Fair correspondent and author of Uncensored Royals, explained why the royal family upheld the motto on most occasions. "Dignified silence is a tried and tested format," she told Time magazine in 2023. "...The palace is reluctant to engage at any level because once they do, it just fuels the narrative." She added, "The Queen only responded when she absolutely had to and it was often short and succinct."

Aside from the Oprah interview and Spencer's new memoir, the royal family has publicly responded on several other notable occasions.

After facing heavy criticism for not returning to London from the family's Balmoral Castle residence in Scotland immediately after Diana's death, the Queen eventually addressed the U.K. in an extraordinary live speech five days later. She referred to herself "as your Queen" and "a grandmother," paid tribute to Diana and said she had remained at Balmoral to help "William and Harry come to terms with the devastating loss that they and the rest of us have suffered."

Andrew attempted to explain his friendship with Jeffrey Epstein and rebut Virginia Giuffre's allegations. The BBC interview was met with intense criticism, and Andrew soon withdrew from royal duties.

In 2025, Buckingham Palace announced that Andrew had been stripped of his prince title and would be moving out of his Royal Lodge home in Windsor, England.

A statement from the palace read, "These censures are deemed necessary, notwithstanding the fact that [Andrew] continues to deny the allegations against him. Their Majesties wish to make clear that their thoughts and utmost sympathies have been, and will remain with, the victims and survivors of any and all forms of abuse."

After The Times of London reported that some former staff members had accused Meghan of bullying, the palace said it was "clearly very concerned" and said its HR team would look into how the complaints were handled. Meghan's representatives denied the allegations.

The three main royal households — Buckingham Palace (which represents the British monarch), Clarence House (Charles's home and communications team) and Kensington Palace (William and Kate's London office and household base) — joined forces to issue a rare rebuttal to a BBC documentary about William and Harry's relationship with the media, calling claims "overblown and unfounded."

The royal aide sparked uproar after repeatedly asking Ngozi Fulani, the founder and chief executive of a U.K. domestic abuse charity, where she "really" came from at a palace reception. Buckingham Palace called the comments "unacceptable and deeply regrettable." Hussey subsequently stepped aside from her honorary role the same day.

Buckingham Palace responded to allegations made by Harry after he lost an appeal over his U.K. security arrangements. Harry said the process had been used to control him and that the royal household had influenced the decision. The palace responded, "All of these issues have been examined repeatedly and meticulously by the courts, with the same conclusion reached on each occasion."

title: Man who sprayed Democratic Rep. Omar with vinegar gets 14 months in prison
description:
— The man who sprayed vinegar at Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors.
The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the Jan.
fullText:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The man who sprayed vinegar at Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors.

The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the Jan. 27 assault. At the time, Minneapolis-St. Paul was facing an immigration crackdown that led to angry protests, arrests and the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal officers.

Kazmierczak was also sentenced to three years of supervised release, which includes no contact with Omar. U.S. marshals escorted him from the courtroom after he was sentenced.

"This wasn't a spur of the moment act," U.S. District Judge Joan N. Ericksen said before handing down the sentence, noting that Kazmierczak had secured tickets for the town hall weeks in advance.

"An attack on a public figure is not a political statement. It is misguided, selfish, and inconsistent with any concept of a free or democratic society," Ericksen said. Spraying anything at an elected official "is a terrifying thing, and you knew that when you did it."

Kazmierczak, who has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, shook visibly at times as he sat at the defense table. He spoke quietly and haltingly, occasionally wiping away tears as he stood before Ericksen.

He spoke about being a good neighbor, and how his troubles with insurance companies as well as prison had exacerbated his ailments. His attorney, John Fossum, argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medications before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened.

"I've spent enough time in jail thinking," Kazmierczak said, his voice barely audible. "I really apologize to her for having put her through that," he said, referring to Omar.

In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions, saying only "it's fuzzy" when Ericksen asked what he remembered.

"I'm sorry if I scared you," he wrote to Omar after the attack.

During the town hall, witnesses saw Kazmierczak jump up from the audience, spraying liquid from a syringe at Omar and saying she was "splitting Minnesota apart." Omar's security officers tackled Kazmierczak and turned him over to police, who arrested him.

Omar was not injured and continued with the town hall after the arrest.

Authorities later determined he had sprayed her with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a U.S. officer.

The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating he planned to do something at the meeting involving Omar "but would not answer their questions about his intent."

He also sent messages to a neighbor to arrange for dog care and asking for bail bond company contact information.

The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse, had "a history of mental and emotional health concerns" and a string of health issues tied to his 2022 Parkinson's disease diagnosis.

Omar, a refugee from Somalia, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's anti-immigrant rhetoric. In 2019, after Omar's election to Congress, Trump said she should "go back" to her country of birth. He has described her as "garbage" and said she should be investigated.

In social media posts, Kazmierczak had criticized former President Joe Biden and referred to Democrats as "angry and liars." He wrote that Trump wants the U.S. to be "stronger and more prosperous."

His attack came as the Minneapolis area was on edge due to the crackdown, with protesters often facing off against convoys of immigration officers and conservatives criticizing protesters.

The story has been corrected to show the sentencing was Thursday, not Wednesday.

title: NBC news chopper's final video captures a troubling sound moments before the crash
description:
Mourners leave notes at a memorial for the NBC4 helicopter crew at Whiteman Airport in Pacoima. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times)
NBC4’s helicopter was one of several news aircraft flying over the scene of a deadly bus crash in Chatsworth on Tuesday evening at sunset.
It’s common for multiple news choppers to arrive at the scene of breaking news, beaming live images for newscasts and streaming.
But around 7 p.m.
fullText:
NBC4's helicopter was one of several news aircraft flying over the scene of a deadly bus crash in Chatsworth on Tuesday evening at sunset.

It's common for multiple news choppers to arrive at the scene of breaking news, beaming live images for newscasts and streaming.

But around 7 p.m., something went horribly wrong. In a matter of seconds, the NBC4 chopper dropped out of the sky, crashing into shipping containers and vehicles outside a warehouse a few blocks away, bursting into flames. Two station journalists, reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, were killed along with a bystander on the ground.

Federal investigators are now trying to figure out what went wrong. The Times interviewed several experts, who reviewed recordings of the chopper's final moments. They offered insights into the helicopter itself, its movements that afternoon and what is known about how its mechanics work.

A video stream from the helicopter, as it was covering the bus crash, appears to show the helicopter hovering just before it came crashing down. An alarm can be heard blaring as the helicopter appears to be quickly losing altitude.

That alarm would be triggered by a potential engine failure, causing low propeller rotation, or a problem with the hydraulic system, said Jack Cress, a former helicopter pilot for the U.S. Marine Corps and a helicopter accident investigation instructor at USC's Aviation Safety and Security Program.

If the helicopter suddenly loses revolutions per minute, or RPMs, there is a safety maneuver known as autorotation, in which the pilot can try to gain enough momentum and upward flow on the rotor blades as it descends and moves laterally to increase rotation and control its landing. But Cress said the fact that the helicopter appeared to be hovering in the air, and at a low altitude, would make it difficult for the pilot to execute the maneuver.

Jeff Guzzetti, a former National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration investigator as well as an instructor in USC's Aviation Safety and Security Program, also believes the horn heard in the video was a low rotor RPM alarm, he said, and that the audio seems to indicate a mechanical problem moments before the crash.

"You can hear something mechanical that is winding down in the background," he said. "It does seem like something mechanical suddenly happened to the helicopter while it was in stable flight."

NTSB investigators have also zeroed in on that recording. In it, the sound of the engine's motor winds down and a horn blares, possibly warning the pilot that the main rotor speed had dropped too low or the helicopter had lost hydraulics. Moreno responds to the noise with a quiet, "Uh-oh."

The angle of the camera begins to descend and Moreno is heard asking, "You can't pull up?" before the video cuts out. Moreno, Marciniw and 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, who was on the ground when the chopper went down, were killed.

"That video is probably the most important piece of evidence we have recovered so far," said NTSB Investigator Fabian Salazar.

Cress compared the autorotation maneuver to a fixed-wing airplane gliding through air with the force generated by its wings, but the helicopter would use the upward force on its rotors caused by descending, or moving forward, to make the rotors turn fast enough to keep itself in the air.

In this case, Cress said, the pilot may not have had that chance.

"He's in the worst part of the height-velocity curve," Cress said, referring to a chart referenced by helicopter pilots that tracks height and air speed for safe flight conditions. "That is a dangerous place to be."

Helicopter pilots are trained to stay away from those conditions, Cress said, because the lack of altitude and forward momentum give them little recourse if there is engine trouble.

But Cress points out that for news helicopters, and police choppers, hovering and maintaining low altitude is a common practice.

Thomas Anthony, director of USC's Aviation Safety and Security Program, said the AS350 B2 helicopter in Tuesday's crash is not only a popular helicopter to see in the skies, but one that is typically very reliable.

It is the most commonly used helicopter for both law enforcement and news gathering, he said, adding that it's "the workhorse of the helicopter fleet."

The helicopter is known for its reliability, is easily fixed when an issue arises, and has a reputation for "robust maintenance support" from its manufacturer, Anthony said.

But the nature of the work in both news and police helicopters increases their risk, Anthony said. While pilots and instructors stress standardizing procedures and flight paths, news incidents such as police chases, fires and crashes force pilots into new conditions during every flight.

The AS350 B2, Cress said, is a reliable model and popular across the globe with a good safety record. But he added some of the features that make the model reliable may have contributed to the crash.

"In 999 out of 1,000 flights, this is a great helicopter," Cress said.

The single-engine and light design is reliable and maintains a good track record, but Cress said any kind of engine failure can also mean there's no secondary engine to help the pilot bring the helicopter down.

The light design of the rotors also means that if there is an engine failure, the light blades can lose their momentum in rotation quickly, Cress said.

Those conditions of hovering in the air, with little altitude and no momentum are commonly referred to by helicopter pilots as a "dead man's curve," said Guzzetti.

"That's the worst place to be if you have a problem," Guzzetti said.

A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times.

title: NASA spacecraft discovers moon crater bigger than Roman Colosseum
description:
Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.
The steep-sided hole measured about 728 feet across, the length of two football fields, and up to 141 feet deep, equivalent to three vertically stacked yellow school buses, according to NASA. It's the solar system's biggest known impact crater carved out in recent times.
Such a large-scale event is estimated to occur only once every 132 years, researchers said, making this a treasure trove of information as NASA prepares to build a base for astronauts on the moon.
"This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation," the scientists wrote in one of two studies appearing on the subject Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.
fullText:
Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.

The steep-sided hole measured about 728 feet across, the length of two football fields, and up to 141 feet deep, equivalent to three vertically stacked yellow school buses, according to NASA. It's the solar system's biggest known impact crater carved out in recent times.

Such a large-scale event is estimated to occur only once every 132 years, researchers said, making this a treasure trove of information as NASA prepares to build a base for astronauts on the moon.

"This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation," the scientists wrote in one of two studies appearing on the subject Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted the crater on the moon's near side sometime between April 11 and May 22, 2024, soon after it was formed when an incoming fragment of an asteroid or comet the size of a three- to six-story building hit the surface. The moon strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space.

LRO's wide-angle images were not identified in the crush of data until August 2025. The spacecraft gathered more detailed pictures last fall, followed by confirmation of the discovery early this year.

The crater — named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston's Lunar and Planetary Institute — is three times bigger than the previous record-holder found by the LRO a decade ago. Pockmarked since ancient times, the moon bears some of the solar system's largest impact craters, including one that stretches more than 1,500 miles across.

This latest impact churned the lunar surface for more than 66 miles. Dust and rocky soil were hurled away at a higher angle than expected, according to Mark Robinson, chief scientist for the LRO's cameras who works at Intuitive Machines. Robinson was the lead author for one of the studies.

A separate study identified a 4-mile-wide cold spot around the new crater, consistent with a loosening of the moon's topsoil. Co-author David Paige of the University of California, Los Angeles, likens it to gardening.

"We're now thinking of impacts as a way to garden the regolith — churning the sediments and putting stuff above that's usually below the surface," Paige said in a statement.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has circled the moon since 2009, providing a close-up view of the lunar surface as the space agency prepares to send astronauts back. The LRO's numerous crater discoveries since its launch show that the moon's top inch of soil is being overturned by ejected material every 80,000 years, faster than previously thought, according to Robinson.

Contrary to the popular belief that the Apollo moonwalkers' dusty lunar footprints will last forever, they will "definitely be long gone in that time frame," Robinson said in an email.

The next step is to calculate the risk of ejected crater material striking NASA's planned moon base, he added. "That information will help engineers harden structures so one won't have to worry about damage, or maybe worry less."

fullText:
Wild courthouse video appears to show a newly sentenced Ohio man slipping out of his handcuffs, punching a bailiff and making a desperate run for the exit before deputies stopped his escape.

Timothy J. Reaggle, 20, of Wellsville, allegedly attacked two Columbiana County Sheriff's Office deputies Monday shortly after learning he would spend a year in prison in a separate case, according to local reports.

Columbiana County Sheriff Brian McLaughlin told WFMJ that both deputies suffered broken bones but have since been released from the hospital.

Video released by the sheriff's office shows a deputy escorting Reaggle down a hallway after his sentencing. Reaggle then suddenly breaks free of his handcuffs and allegedly punches the deputy before sprinting away.

As he runs down the hallway, Reaggle is seen crashing into another deputy, knocking him to the ground.

Reaggle then allegedly headed toward the courthouse exit, where video shows him sliding down the steps and racing toward the front doors before he was subdued with a Taser and taken into custody.

The video also shows people rushing to assist the injured deputies. One deputy was later seen lying on the floor, bleeding from the head and holding a paper towel against his face, according to WFMJ.

Reaggle had just been sentenced to one year in prison in a case dating to Feb. 14, 2025, according to WKBN.

He pleaded guilty in July to charges including aggravated burglary, aggravated assault, aggravated menacing, failure to comply and two misdemeanor counts of assault.
