title: Trump slashed DEI. Now it's making a surprising bipartisan comeback.
description:
Political pressure during the Trump era forced corporate America to put its diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives on ice. 
Now, in a surprising turn, growing rank-and-file buy-in is driving a quiet thaw across party lines, with even Republican employees expressing approval for such workplace programs.
This unexpected bipartisan support for DEI emerged in the latest Bentley University-Gallup Business in Society survey provided exclusively to USA TODAY. Though views remain deeply polarized, workers across the ideological spectrum are growing more positive about the workplace benefits of diversity programs.
Nearly three-quarters (72%) of Americans believe promoting DEI should be a priority for businesses.
fullText:
Political pressure during the Trump era forced corporate America to put its diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives on ice.

Now, in a surprising turn, growing rank-and-file buy-in is driving a quiet thaw across party lines, with even Republican employees expressing approval for such workplace programs.

This unexpected bipartisan support for DEI emerged in the latest Bentley University-Gallup Business in Society survey provided exclusively to USA TODAY. Though views remain deeply polarized, workers across the ideological spectrum are growing more positive about the workplace benefits of diversity programs.

Nearly three-quarters (72%) of Americans believe promoting DEI should be a priority for businesses. What's more, public faith in the bottom-line benefits of diversity is climbing as more Americans link diverse workforces to increased profitability and innovation than at any point in the past two years.

The findings defy expectations in today's political climate and even surprised researchers.

President Donald Trump took office pledging to eliminate "woke" Biden-era policies that he argues elevate race and gender above merit. The administration's crackdown has sent shockwaves through the corporate world.

Fearing federal investigations and lost government contracts, major U.S. companies rushed to dismantle their diversity initiatives. In the latest sign of escalating enforcement, the Justice Department announced this week that Accenture will pay $25 million to resolve allegations that its employment practices violated federal anti-discrimination rules.

Yet three-quarters of the Bentley University-Gallup survey respondents said businesses with diverse workforces make more innovative products, up from 64% in 2025. Seventy-one percent of Americans say it is somewhat or completely true that businesses with diverse workforces are more profitable, up from 61% in 2025.

The survey highlights the enduring partisan divide over DEI, though the ideological gap has noticeably narrowed, according to Cynthia Clark, a member of the Bentley-Gallup survey's research team.

Nearly all Democrats (95%) consider promoting DEI a key business priority with 71% of independents in agreement, though far fewer Republicans held the same view (37%).

Among Democrats, 92% say businesses with diverse workforces are more profitable, up from 85% in 2025. The percentage also rose 11 points among independents (70%) and Republicans (41%).

The survey found widespread agreement that workforce diversity fuels product innovation, supported by 94% of Democrats, 75% of Independents and nearly half of Republicans. Those figures are up six, 12 and 11 points, respectively, from 2025.

A double-digit surge in support across party lines points to a growing rift between rank-and-file workers and corporate leaders pulling back from DEI, said Clark, a Bentley University management professor.

“This should be a signal to managers to look internally to their employees for what works at their firm rather than following the political flavor of the moment,” she said.

Despite softening resistance, skepticism persists among Republicans. Over half say it is somewhat or completely untrue that businesses with diverse workforces are more profitable (59%) or that they make more innovative products (54%).

The findings also expose a gap between what Americans expect from businesses and what those companies actually deliver, according to Clark.

Only a third of Americans rate corporate DEI performance as good or excellent, reflecting a dissatisfaction that also split along party lines.

While half of Republicans gave companies high marks, that approval dropped to roughly a third among independents and just a quarter among Democrats.

title: Scientists discover the first new cat species in more than 100 years
description:
In 2016, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a biologist and National Geographic Explorer working in Bolivia, received a call from a local wildlife sanctuary that had just been given what they described as “a weird cat.” It came from a local man who found it as a kitten on a road near a forest. The man took the animal home, believing it to be a domestic breed. But after about a year of living with the clearly wild animal, he realized it would be better off at a sanctuary.
As the lead scientist and founder of the Bolivian Felids Research Program (Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia), Nogales-Ascarrunz was intrigued.
fullText:
In 2016, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a biologist and National Geographic Explorer working in Bolivia, received a call from a local wildlife sanctuary that had just been given what they described as “a weird cat.” It came from a local man who found it as a kitten on a road near a forest. The man took the animal home, believing it to be a domestic breed. But after about a year of living with the clearly wild animal, he realized it would be better off at a sanctuary.

As the lead scientist and founder of the Bolivian Felids Research Program (Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia), Nogales-Ascarrunz was intrigued. The animal had a small, scrunched-up face, short and round ears, and long whiskers. It was, indeed, too small to be a housecat, and, most notably, it was covered in leopard-like spots. So she went to visit the creature at the Senda Verde wildlife sanctuary on the subtropical flank of the Bolivian Andes.

“I took a hundred pictures of it,” remembers Nogales-Ascarrunz. “I was so fascinated.”

What she couldn’t know at the time was that this curious cat had a secret. It would become the first new species of felid (i.e. the cat family) discovered in over 100 years, according to a study published today in the journal Current Biology. What’s exciting is the discovery is not a validation of a species proposed in the distant past, nor a previously recognized subspecies raised to species status—which are both more commonly reported and important findings. No, this cat was something totally new to science.

At the time though, Nogales-Ascarrunz assumed the unusual cat was a member of the species Leopardus tigrinus. Sometimes called tigrinas, oncillas, tigrillos, or little spotted cats, this species was described back in 1775 from a single illustration of an animal seen in French Guiana and was subsequently presumed to exist across Central and South America, including, at the time, Bolivia.

But then in 2019, while she was preparing a booklet about Bolivia’s cat species, she realized the cat she’d photographed didn’t look like a guidebook reference photo from neighboring Brazil. Her tiger cat had rosettes that were much larger than the ones across the border. “This is so wrong,” she thought.

It would take another few years before Nogales-Ascarrunz developed her skills in genetic analysis to the point where she could investigate the mystery cat’s genome with any accuracy. Then, working with Eduardo Eizirik, a geneticist at Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil, and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart from the University of Antwerp, the team was able to find its distinct place on the cat family tree.

In their paper, the researchers propose the cat should be known as Leopardus tilcayo, in honor of the word local people know it by. "We asked the local people, ‘Why do you call it tilcayo?’” says Nogales-Ascarrunz, who is herself from Bolivia. “And they said, ‘I don’t know! My grandpa called it tilcayo, so I call it tilcayo.” (The name does not appear to mean anything particular in Spanish or the Quechua language spoken in Bolivia.)

So far, all scientists can say is that L. tilcayo lives in Bolivia’s Yungas forest ecoregion, which lies on the eastern slope of the Andes Mountains. But as to what these cats eat or get eaten by, how they reproduce, and many other facets of their day-to-day lives, much mystery remains. “So many basic things are not known,” says Nogales-Ascarrunz, who is co-lead author of the new study.

But the discovery is monumental, and not just because it’s the first new cat discovered since the pampas cat in 1923. The new paper doesn’t just name a new species; it redraws the cat family tree to have a lot more branches than previously thought. What’s more, the researchers hope the methods used to identify L. tilcayo may soon be used to find even more cat species spread across the world, and even transform how we protect them.

While physical differences such as tail length, rosette size, or teeth shape are always important indicators for scientists looking to delineate species, genomic analyses are increasingly the gold standard, simply because they can tell a story hidden from the naked eye.

“We’ve been working on tiger cats for 25 years or so, trying to sort out the whole genus, Leopardes,” says Eizirik. The deeper these scientists look into these cat’s genomes, the more hidden variation they find.

In 2013, scientists provided evidence that Leopardus tigrinus — the species Nogales-Ascarrunz originally assumed the new cat to be a member of — were actually made up of two distinct species. Then in 2024, the landscape changed again with the proposal that another genetically distinct species be peeled off from the previous two. Now, the newest study makes five tiger cat species. “What we once thought to be a single species, we’ve started to see that it was actually a species complex,” Eizirik says.

While this kind of confusion would be unheard of in, say, the Panthera genus — which includes cats such as tigers, snow leopards, and lions — the world’s small wild cats are much less studied. They are also exceptionally good at remaining out of sight. Even photos taken by remote trail cameras may not provide enough evidence to distinguish the species. For instance, one of the museum specimens included in the new study was originally thought to be another small, spotted cat called a margay, until it was later identified as a tiger cat (L. tigrinus) due to the direction of its nape hairs.

Modern genomics lets scientists see deeper differences photographs and fieldnotes miss. In the new study, when the researchers compared complete genomes from 38 individuals across the Leopardus genus, the results showed that not only was L. tilcayo different from the other tiger cat species, but it had diverged from them around 1.4 million years ago—an evolutionary distance comparable to that between modern lions and extinct cave lions.

While the discovery of yet another new tiger cat “is itself surprising news, the results obtained profoundly change how small cat specialists group small cat species in genus Leopardus,” says James Sanderson, founder and director of the Small Wild Cat Conservation Foundation who was not an author on the new publication. To that end, the study also provides evidence for a new sub-species of tiger cat in Peru, Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo, and according to Sanderson, its findings also hint that the margay—which scientists have assumed to be one species spread across Mexico through Argentina— is not one species, but four.

“This study hints that, having split from a common ancestor close to [one million years ago], four distinct margay species exist,” says Sanderson, who is also a member of the IUCN Cat Specialist Group, in an email. For his part, Eizirik says a more focused study of margay genetics will be needed before he’d make such a claim.

Sanderson says this is likely just the beginning of more discoveries. “It’s by no means a stretch of the imagination that the improved methods used in this study will reveal new species of small wild cats in Africa and Asia,” he says.

All of these additional branches on the cat family tree will have real world consequences for conservation.

One of the key factors to establish a species’ conservation status is its geographic distribution. “If you think [the tiger cat] is a single thing from southern Brazil all the way to Costa Rica, you’re going to find it’s not endangered,” says Eizirik. “But if we find that it’s not a single thing, but actually five things, each of them must be assessed separately.”

According to Sanderson, such distinctions add urgency to conservation efforts. “Once three species become five species, each population is reduced,” he says. “Therefore conservation efforts must increase, perhaps urgently, depending on estimated population sizes.” (For now, scientists are unsure of how many tilcayos exist in the wild.)

Genetics and questions of taxonomy aside, Nogales-Ascarrunz doesn’t want to lose focus on the wonder. “Our world is extremely complex,” she says. “Sometimes we think that most of it is known, that there's not a whole lot to discover, but in fact, it's the other way around.”

It is now commonplace for scientists to announce the discovery of new species, though the description of new insects, microbes, and other small organisms dominates the literature. And that makes sense, because they are easily hidden, hard to find, and often evade our understanding. But a five-pound felid?

“Even in the cats, there are things out there that are undescribed, things that people haven't found yet,” says Nogagles-Ascarrunz. “So let's go out and find them and protect them.”

title: Judge sets new condition as Trump talks about Kennedy Center being 'ripped down'
description:
A federal judge ordered President Donald Trump's administration on Thursday to provide at least 30 days' notice before taking any steps to demolish the Kennedy Center, the landmark performing arts venue ‌that has become a flashpoint in his efforts to reshape the U.S. capital. 
   U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 (Reuters) - A federal judge ordered President Donald Trump's administration on Thursday to provide at least 30 days' notice before taking any steps to demolish the Kennedy Center, the landmark performing arts venue ‌that has become a flashpoint in his efforts to reshape the U.S. capital.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued the order after ‌lawyers for a Democratic congresswoman who is suing to keep the venue open and Trump's name off its facade submitted new evidence citing the Republican president's comments on Wednesday referring ​to demolishing the Kennedy Center.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down," Trump told reporters in North Carolina, referring to putting his name on the facility established by Congress and opened in 1971 as a memorial to slain President John Kennedy.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's Trump-backed executive director, said in a court filing earlier on Thursday that ‌the building was being temporarily closed to assess safety ⁠risks in areas "exhibiting severe structural deterioration."

Democratic U.S. Representative Joyce Beatty, who sued Trump last year over his Kennedy Center plans, responded in a filing in federal court in Washington that the closure "is a recipe for defendants extending their ⁠shutdown forever and closing the Kennedy Center for the next two years — the very thing this court said they could not do without its permission."

Beatty's lawyers also cited a photo circulating on social media that depicted the president aboard Air Force One looking at a poster they said appeared to be titled "Kennedy ​Center ​DEMOLISHED." The photo has not been independently verified by Reuters.

Trump last year had the ​White House's historic East Wing demolished to make way for ‌a ballroom project he has pursued.

Cooper turned down a request by Beatty for an emergency hearing on her lawsuit after the Kennedy Center's board, including Trump and his hand-picked appointees, voted this week to close the venue for up to two years for a $257 million renovation project.

Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's board, said the venue is no longer accessible to the public during normal operating hours. New barriers were visible outside the building on Wednesday.

Beatty and other critics have accused Trump of seeking to place his name on the Kennedy ‌Center out of vanity. Trump's name had been placed on the building's facade ​until the judge in May ordered it removed, saying only Congress can change the ​name.

Cooper earlier directed the board to explain by Thursday whether the administration's ​plan violates an earlier order he issued limiting its ability to shut its doors. The board said on ‌Thursday morning that it was not in violation of the ​order, and the seven-day emergency closure ​was separate from the larger renovation plans.

The Trump administration said it would ask the judge by Friday to dissolve the prior order to allow for what the government called "closure necessary to complete the restoration and renovations."

Cooper, in a ruling on Tuesday, rejected the center's latest ​effort to put Trump's name on the building ‌to reflect his role in the planned renovation. The administration has appealed, and Trump said on social media the Kennedy ​Center "is destined to doom" if it is not permitted to close for repairs.

title: White House withdraws ICE director nominee after Republican blocks hearing
description:
The White House on Thursday withdrew the nomination of Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement after a Republican blocked his confirmation hearing.
Schroyer’s nomination stalled after Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.), a foe of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, requested that the Department of Homeland Security provide his committee with more information about its investigation into two ICE and Border Patrol agents accused of killing two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January.
fullText:
The White House on Thursday withdrew the nomination of Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement after a Republican blocked his confirmation hearing.

Schroyer's nomination stalled after Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.), a foe of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, requested that the Department of Homeland Security provide his committee with more information about its investigation into two ICE and Border Patrol agents accused of killing two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January.

Paul, who as chair controls the committee's hearing and markup agenda, did not oppose Schroyer's nomination, per Drew Carmichael, a spokesperson for the senator.

Schroyer was a surprise pick to lead ICE. He had no experience leading a major law enforcement agency, let alone an organization the size of ICE. But Schroyer has close ties with the DHS secretary. Schroyer at one point led Mullin's security detail and Mullin made Schroyer a senior adviser at DHS.

The White House and DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The nomination's withdrawal is a blow to Mullin, who has faced criticism from immigration hardliners over what they have characterized as insufficient progress in achieving mass deportations of unauthorized immigrants from the United States. Mullin had defended his pick to lead ICE, saying he wanted someone who could be confirmed in the Senate.

Mullin's pitch for putting Schroyer in the role in part involved highlighting his experience with helping stand up special units in the Oklahoma Highway Patrol to locate abducted children, as well as his work implementing a state program allowing local police departments to work with ICE on arresting undocumented immigrants.

But immigration hardliners weren't convinced. They and others in the administration doubted Schroyer could lead the complex agency — or even clear the Senate.

Schroyer's abrupt exit means the agency's streak of not having a confirmed leader at the top ranks will continue. The Senate has not confirmed an ICE director since 2014 and there is pessimism within the administration's ranks that the Senate could confirm any nominee with a significant track record at ICE, given how polarizing the agency has become under President Donald Trump.

Acting ICE chief David Venturella, a close ally of White House border czar Tom Homan, has led ICE while Schroyer's nomination was pending. Under federal law, as long as a nominee is pending Venturella can serve in that role indefinitely. Now, the clock starts ticking on a 210 day limit for his tenure, unless someone else is nominated.

Venturella would have his own challenges if he were nominated for the role, including past work for GEO Group, a major private detention company. Some in the administration have said that association would hurt his chances at confirmation to lead ICE in Schroyer's place.

title: Trump's rate hike comments place renewed scrutiny on the Fed's independence
description:
President Donald Trump with Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh at the White House in Washington, DC, on May 22. - Jonathan Ernst/Reuters/File
The Federal Reserve’s first rate hike in three years has ushered in a new twist to the already unusual relationship between President Donald Trump and the world’s most powerful central bank.
Trump raised eyebrows on Wednesday evening by appearing to suggest that he gave Kevin Warsh, his handpicked Fed chairman, permission to raise rates – even though it was the “wrong” move. The president implied that Warsh had no choice but to embrace a rate increase because the Fed chief was outnumbered on the “hostile” rate-setting committee he oversees.
“I talked to Kevin and I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter…I said, ‘Do what you want because it doesn’t matter’ because he doesn’t have the votes,” Trump told reporters.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve’s first rate hike in three years has ushered in a new twist to the already unusual relationship between President Donald Trump and the world’s most powerful central bank.

Trump raised eyebrows on Wednesday evening by appearing to suggest that he gave Kevin Warsh, his handpicked Fed chairman, permission to raise rates – even though it was the “wrong” move. The president implied that Warsh had no choice but to embrace a rate increase because the Fed chief was outnumbered on the “hostile” rate-setting committee he oversees.

“I talked to Kevin and I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter…I said, ‘Do what you want because it doesn’t matter’ because he doesn’t have the votes,” Trump told reporters.

The remarks raise plenty of questions about how much – if at all – Warsh is consulting with a president who has been willing to cross red lines in his quest for dramatically lower interest rates.

Those questions are especially sensitive because the Fed is designed to be insulated from the political winds in Washington. Central bankers are required to make trillion-dollar decisions on whether to raise or lower interest rates based on what’s best for the economy, not for the political party in power.

Tellingly, some Fed watchers and former officials reacted to the remarks with disbelief.

“It’s an unusual and unfortunate comment to make. Clearly, the Fed chair does not need the president’s permission to raise rates,” Eric Rosengren, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, told CNN on Thursday. “The implication is that the chair got a hall pass. I have no idea how truthful the comment was.”

Krishna Guha, vice chairman and head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI who criticized Warsh’s initial stumbles, dismissed Trump’s claims.

“The market believes – and with good grounds – that Kevin Warsh owned this decision and that the committee was strongly united behind him,” Guha said. “There is no evidence here or to the market at large that Warsh was dragged into this by colleagues – or permissioned by the president.”

The risk is that Trump fuels suspicions that swirled on Wall Street this summer that Warsh may not be truly independent. That’s dangerous because a Fed doing the White House’s bidding could lose control of market-set interest rates, dramatically increasing the cost of mortgages and car loans. And a loss of faith in Fed independence could unhinge inflation expectations among investors and consumers.

The Fed declined to comment to CNN about Trump’s remarks.

For his part, Warsh tap-danced around questions related to the man who nominated him.

“I’m not a Wall Street newsletter. Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street,” Warsh said during the press conference on Wednesday. “We’ll let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane, too. That’s how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them.”

Asked by a reporter when he last spoke with the president, Warsh said: “I don’t have anything for you on discussions with the president.”

Tim Mahedy, CEO and chief economist at research firm Access/Macro, said he found that response from Warsh “strange.”

“The right answer is, ‘I didn’t talk to the president.’ I don’t think the president is talking to Warsh beforehand. That would be shocking,” said Mahedy, a former official at the IMF and San Francisco Fed.

The other risk is that, intentionally or not, Trump diminishes Warsh as an ineffectual leader – just as he appeared to be starting to find his footing.

“It makes it seem like Warsh has no control over this committee, like he was completely ineffectual in convincing his colleagues,” said Mahedy.

Warsh emerged from the meeting looking independent. Not only did he preside over a rate hike the White House did not want, but he explained it clearly and with the unanimous support of his colleagues – including former Fed Chair Jerome Powell.

“It felt like the day the Fed became Warsh’s Fed,” Evercore’s Guha said. “He was a lot more assured, coherent and credible yesterday. What he’s saying basically adds up.”

But now if Warsh and a majority of his colleagues on the committee decide against a rate hike, he will face questions about whether the president put his finger on the scale.

In the past, most presidents have gone out of their way to even avoid the appearance of interfering with the Fed because it was widely accepted that an independent Fed builds confidence.

None of this is to say Trump unleashed on the Fed in a way that would have unnerved investors. In fact, Trump’s initial reaction to the first rate hike under Warsh was relatively mild, especially compared with his relentless and deeply personal condemnation of Powell, his last handpicked Fed chair.

While Trump bashed Warsh’s colleagues as “very hostile” and “very political,” he singled out the Fed chief for praise. “He’s a good man, Kevin Warsh,” Trump said.

“People were fearful of a fierce backlash from the president against this decision to raise rates and a resumption of the conflict between the White House and the Fed,” Guha said.

Of course, the Warsh-Trump relationship will continue to evolve, likely guided by what happens next to inflation, borrowing costs and the path of the S&P 500 and all-important Treasury rates.

Mahedy said he worries that the relationship will break down if the Warsh-led Fed continues to raise rates – as many suspect it will be forced to.

“It’s not hard to see more blame being put on the Fed and Warsh – and then it will start to look a lot like Powell,” said Mahedy. “It’s kind of a train wreck – but a slow-moving one.”

Glasner on Milenkovic, City Ground plans and Coventry
description: Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner has been speaking to the media before Saturday's Premier League game against Coventry City at the City Ground (kick-off 17:30 BST).  Nikola Milenkovic will miss the game, while fellow defender Jair Cunha trained on Thursday and "looks OK", though Glasner added that it was a "very light session".  Glasner described planning approval for the development of the City Ground as "great news for the club, the city and the supporters".
fullText:
Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner has been speaking to the media before Saturday's Premier League game against Coventry City at the City Ground (kick-off 17:30 BST).

Here are the key lines from his news conference:

Nikola Milenkovic will miss the game, while fellow defender Jair Cunha trained on Thursday and "looks OK", though Glasner added that it was a "very light session".

Glasner described planning approval for the development of the City Ground as "great news for the club, the city and the supporters".

Asked if he expected to still be at the club when the works are complete, he said: "I never think about leaving. You don't start a relationship and think about when you can leave. It makes no sense. I'm always thinking mid- and long-term. If somebody asks me how I see things, I always try to look a little bit outside of football."

On last weekend's win at Aston Villa: "It was good out of possession but it was maximum OK in possession and I would say below average in possession in the first half. Of course, when you win and when you show a good performance it helps in getting more and more belief, getting more and more confidence."

On Morgan Gibbs-White and whether he should receive an England call-up having missed out on the World Cup squad: "I think he showed maximum effort, commitment and good performances. It's Thomas Tuchel's decision."

Glasner said he spent some time with Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis: "Sometimes you are emotional during a game, this is what I talked about to him, because he's also quite emotional. I don't talk to the players after the game. It makes no sense - because then maybe you regret it the following day."

The Austrian said Saturday's opponents Coventry, who are yet to register a point or score a goal in the league, will pose "the same challenges we have faced and will face in every Premier League game". He added: "They are a good team with a fantastic manager. They played a great Championship season. They had quite a tough schedule at the beginning [of this season]."

On the upcoming international break: "We decided to give the players the first week off. It's quite difficult to keep the motivation high when you know there is no competitive game in the mid-season. Then, in the second week, we will start having a normal training week with a friendly game on Saturday. Then, in the third week, hopefully all internationals will come back well without any injuries. Then we prepare for Crystal Palace."

title: Seahawks vs Cardinals: Week 2 score prediction
description: Predicting the outcome of the Seahawks vs Arizona matchup for Week 2 of the NFL season.
fullText:
Week 2 is upon us! After a Week 1 victory over the New England Patriots, the Seattle Seahawks now travel to Glendale for the first divisional rivalry game versus the Arizona Cardinals. In this battle of the birds, who will come out the victor? Will the Seahawks set a franchise record and get their 12th straight win? Or will the Cardinals end their losing streak against the Seahawks? Let's try to predict this game!

The Seahawks in their home opener scored 13 points while holding the Patriots to 10 points in the Super Bowl rematch. It seems as though, defensively, the Seahawks have not missed a beat. They struggled a bit offensively, but between Sam Darnold going down five snaps in, and having a first time play-caller calling their first regular season game, that is to be expected. In 2025, they scored an average of 29 points per game, while allowing and average 17 points per game. Averaging the points for comes out to 21 points, while averaging the points allowed comes to 14 points.

Per FTN's DVOA, the Seahawks are the ninth ranked team in total DVOA. They were the 20th ranked offense per DVOA, the fifth ranked defense, and the fourth ranked special teams. It's worth noting that DVOA takes several weeks into the season before it becomes a more stable metric. There's also no accounting for Seattle having Drew Lock come into the game due to Sam Darnold's injury.

Per Sumer Sports, the Seahawks were the 14th ranked offense in total EPA and EPA per play. On defense, they were the 11th ranked defense in total EPA and the 12th ranked defense in EPA per play.

The Cardinals put up 26 in their upset road win over the Los Angeles Chargers. They held Justin Herbert and the Chargers offense to just 14 points. Arizona looked good in its first game of the season, and it seems first-year head coach Mike LaFleur has the team buttoned up. Last season, the Cardinals averaged 22 points a game while allowing opponents to score 29 points. Their overall average points for is 24, while their averaged points allowed is 22.

Per DVOA, the Cardinals were ranked the 13th best team in the NFL after Week One. They had the sixth ranked offense per DVOA, 20th ranked defense, and 18th ranked special teams.

Per Sumer Sports, the Cardinals have the 10th ranked team per total EPA on offense as well as EPA per play on offense. They were also the fifth ranked team per total EPA on defense and fifth in EPA per play on defense.

Seahawks 21 + Cards opponents 22 = 43 / 2 = 21.5 Points for Seahawks, but since you cannot have half a point, lets round up to 22.

Cards 24 + Sea opponents 14 = 38 / 2 = 19 Points for Seahawks

Seahawks score 7 more points on average than opponents. 19 – 4 = 15.

Initial score prediction: 22 – 15, Seahawks win

However, to make this score work, the Seahawks would need to go for a 2-point conversion, and that doesn't make a ton of sense, so let's make some adjustments.

Three touchdowns for the Seahawks make sense. I think Jaxon Smith-Njigba and AJ Barner are likely to get one apiece, and I think Jadarian Price will get his first touchdown in this game. Add those points together with some Jason Myers extra points, and we get 21.

Final Score Prediction: 21 – 15, Seahawks Victory

I went into more detail on the matchup over on The Hawks Eye Podcast. Be sure to check it out here:

How do you think the matchup will turn out? Comment down below, and let's have a discussion. Go Hawks!

title: How Ethan Salas made MLB history for Padres with two-HR night
description: The 20-year-old catcher just made some impressive HR history.
fullText:
How Ethan Salas made MLB history for Padres with two-HR night originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The San Diego Padres recently called up Ethan Salas, their 20-year-old catcher who's been in the headlines for a while now as one of the best young prospects in baseball.

After a down season, he recently turned things around and is now one of the best youngsters in the Majors. Against the Colorado Rockies on Wednesday, Salas made some MLB history that might not be broken for a very long time.

As MLB.com's AJ Cassavell shared, Salas just became the youngest catcher in MLB history to hit two home runs in one game. There has never been a catcher younger than Salas to hit two homers in a game.

"At 20 years, 107 days old, Salas became the youngest catcher in MLB history with two home runs in the same game," Cassavell writes. "He's the youngest Padre at any position to do so."

Being the youngest Padres hitter to have a two-homer game is a very impressive statistic, but expanding it to all MLB history and all catchers, this is quite the feat.

Catchers younger than Salas have hit home runs before, but no catcher in MLB history has ever hit two home runs in the same game while being younger than Salas at 20 years and 107 days old.

MORE: Padres predicted to lose Michael King with $58M opt-out likely

In recent MLB history, Cassavell shared that only Manny Machado, Bryce Harper, Juan Soto, and Mike Trout have hit multiple homers in a game and have been younger than Salas.

That's some great company to be in, as they're all future Hall of Famers, if they've not already locked up a spot the moment they retire.

Salas has a lot of work to do to catch those players, but this two-homer night against the Rockies is a good starting point, as it made some impressive MLB history.

title: Week 2 Fantasy Football Rankings: TE, K, DEF
description: Ranking and evaluating all of Week 2's top plays at tight end, kicker, and defense.
fullText:
Tyler Warren readies for a rough matchup with the Chiefs, Isaiah Likely ponders if this is his long-sought arrival, and Harold Fannin Jr. aims to get something going in his rough offensive environment.

Other positions: Quarterback | Running Back | Receiver

TE Notes: All you can do is laugh when it comes to Colston Loveland's "zero heard 'round the world." By far Loveland's most important Week 1 data point was the Bears' 59 points. If this offense improves on last year — which there is every reason to believe it will — Loveland will still coast to elite TE1 value. … Tyler Warren "ran all the routes" in Week 1. He just didn't catch much of anything during the Colts' dismal offensive showing. Better days should be ahead, though it's worth noting that might not include Week 2 against the Chiefs' strong defense. … Dalton Kincaid is one of my primary "you have to have some reaction" to Week 1 players. We thought — I guess more hoped — the Bills would be a more pass-happy team in Sean McDermott's absence. Were they ever in Houston. … Isaiah Likely is another player where there's no point in pretending we did not see what we saw in Week 1. He's the Giants' No. 2 weapon. He commanded targets and knew what to do with them. You can quibble with the exact rank, but not his clear-cut TE1 status.

Tucker Kraft looked healthy and explosive against the Vikings. With the biggest questions answered, the only remaining query is the date of his first spiked week. … George Kittle wasn't quite as convincing with his Week 1 health, playing under 50 percent of the 49ers' snaps. Although he did not look sluggish, he did not necessarily appear "all the way back," either. Hopefully it was a rust-knocking effort, one for which Kittle will have had nine days to recover from by the time the 49ers face the Dolphins' bottom-barrel defense this Sunday. … It seems like I didn't want to believe Dallas Goedert would remain a TE1, so I just pretended it wouldn't happen. It did, and there was very little evidence to suggest in Week 1 Goedert will find himself outside the top 12 any time soon. … Michael Mayer's Week 1 usage was through the roof in Brock Bowers' (knee) absence, and he responded by leading the Raiders' receivers/tight ends in essentially every category. Bowers is trying to fast track his return, but Mayer will be a usable 12-team league player for however long the big dog remains sidelined.

Mark Andrews appeared neither "back" nor so far gone in the opener. With the Ravens' receiver woes, he will undoubtedly continue to see TE10-14 usage. … Travis Kelce looked like a center trying to advance a fumble on his big Week 1 catch-and-run, but it's clear the Chiefs continue to lack better options in the passing game. Kelce will absorb looks on the TE1/2 borderline and hopefully actually house a few of them for six. … Week 1 was as concerning as it gets for Harold Fannin. Deshaun Watson was as bad as feared, and first-rounder KC Concepcion was as involved as expected. Fannin isn't going to simply disappear as a second-year pro, but his TE1 production can no longer be taken for granted. He's a borderline option in this awful offensive setup. … Tight end is not deep enough to issue a blanket directive like "bench Kyle Pitts for however long Miachel Penix Jr. remains sidelined." But he is certainly not a "must start" in Cooper Rush's presence. If you're looking for something nice to say, it's that another zero is highly unlikely.

title: Week 2 Fantasy Football Rankings: WR
description: Ranking and evaluating all of Week 2's top plays at receiver.
fullText:
DeVonta Smith welcomes a bounce-back matchup in the Titans, Jaxon Smith-Njigba looks to make life easy for Drew Lock, and Christian Watson and Matthew Golden vie for the title of "biggest breakout" in the Packers receiver corps.

Other positions: Quarterback | Running Back | Tight End/Kickers/Defense

WR Notes: Zay Flowers was one of the biggest stories of Week 1. So naturally he picked up a hamstring issue in the process. Officially "DNP" to begin the week on Wednesday, he is looking on the wrong side of questionable to face the Saints. With intriguing rookie Ja'Kobi Lane on IR with a wrist injury, Flowers' absence would leave the Ravens without a viable 12-team league receiver. … It's a year that ends in a number, so Nico Collins is already battling a soft-tissue injury, this time a hamstring. We can't really cling to the fact he was listed as "limited" as opposed to "DNP" on Wednesday because he suffered the injury during practice. He is looking questionable, at best, for what was supposed to be a shootout with the Bengals. … Week 1 was all we needed to see out of DJ Moore. He was elite from every "percentage" and "share" perspective, and even if the Bills' pass-happy Week 1 approach was a bit outlier-ish, it should hold for at least one more week against the shootout-in-a-can Lions. … That was not the opener DeVonta Smith was looking for. There was also zero indication anything was amiss under the hood. He just didn't have a productive game. Those will come in short order.

Week 1 was already enough to rocket Garrett Wilson back up the WR2 rankings into WR1/2 territory. It's not so much that Geno Smith is the world's biggest upgrade — upgrade though he is — but that the Jets' offensive line and coaching environment also appear far less chaotic than a season ago. And Wilson is the kind of player who has provided WR1-type returns whenever he is in a stable environment, even if it's not an elite one. … Malik Nabers keeps claiming he legitimately did not know if he would play in Week 1. Well he not only played, he featured. Nabers' protestations probably contain a kernel of truth since he took the field for just 36-of-69 snaps, but that is a solid baseline set to rapidly increase. … We were looking for signs Christian Watson was finally ready to break out. Consider the best overall game of his career a sign. There will still be a boom/bust element to Watson's game, but both his floor and ceiling should be significantly higher in this condensed target tree.

No good deed goes unpunished. The thanks Tetairoa McMillan got for his sterling rookie campaign was a continued Jalen Coker breakout. Then the thanks Coker got was an immediate ankle injury. Thankfully, Coker appears set to play against the Falcons after getting in a limited practice on Wednesday. Coach Dave Canales confirmed as much afterwards. All of this is good and well, though fantasy managers must remember "@ATL" is not as hospitable of a matchup as it appears since Bryce Young has a tendency of playing up and down to his game situations. Coming off the shootout to end all shootouts, this game has a mediocre 43.5 total. … Parker Washington was the Jaguars' clear-cut WR1 in a noncompetitive Week 1 contest. Week 2 will have a tougher opponent and game environment, but there is no real reason to park Washington outside the top 24 receivers. … It's quite possible the Chiefs' Rashee Rice scam is post-peak. I also think Kenneth Walker III's emergence could be a good thing. Rice is a one-dimensional player. This is now a two-dimensional offense. That lessens the defensive pressure on Rice. Even as someone who never passes up an opportunity to criticize this fake WR1, I know there is every reason to believe better PPR days will be ahead.

Comparing Jaylen Waddle's Week 1 no-show to Colston Loveland's is apples to oranges, but the diagnosis is the same: That's not going to happen too often, and you just have to move on. … The Falcons don't know who their Week 2 quarterback is going to be, ergo I don't know what my Drake London ranking is going to be. I just know it doesn't matter who is under center. I can't go into Sunday afternoon with London on my bench. … Jameson Williams aced every Week 1 test except for the pesky "just catch the damn ball." I will keep the top 24 faith. … Perhaps unsurprisingly, Luther Burden found himself somewhat eased into the season in Week 1. He escaped without issue with regards to the hamstring he pulled in August, and is positioned nicely for another potential shootout with the Vikings. … God save the King, but Quentin Johnston is a must start if Ladd McConkey (ribs) sits, as is looking quite likely. … Trickier is the case of Tre' Harris. Through 18 NFL games, it's unclear what exactly Harris does well. For fantasy, we only care that he's out there for almost every play with Mike McDaniel calling the shots and Justin Herbert delivering the ball. Harris is a credible WR4/5 if you are already in an injury bind.

Even with the Packers' condensed target tree, Matthew Golden's 12 targets were one of the biggest Week 1 surprises to me. It doesn't really matter what you think of a player's talent, draft position, etc. if they are getting 10-plus looks in the opener after the team had an entire offseason to plan for the game. That's a certified commitment. … The Commanders had a lot less time to plan for Stef Diggs' debut and still made him the focal point of their passing attack. That figures to ebb and flow with Terry McLaurin, but Diggs has certainly earned a spot in the top 36. … De'Zhaun Stribling's long-term injury shores up Deebo Samuel inside the top 40, perhaps even with room to grow if he's actually healthy. … You don't overreact to one game but you must react, etc. I don't see how anyone can continue to rank Marvin Harrison Jr. ahead of Michael Wilson for the time being. … Romeo Doubs had the worst ever Week 1 … that the Patriots and fantasy managers just have to shake off. A.J. Brown's absence frees up enough looks to make Doubs worth a look in the top 40.

title: Northwestern extends football coach David Braun's contract through the 2031 season
description: Northwestern has extended coach David Braun’s contract through the 2031 season.  Financial terms weren’t released.  Braun is in his fourth season at Northwestern and carries a 20-19 record into Saturday’s game with Colorado.
fullText:
EVANSTON, Ill. (AP) — Northwestern has extended coach David Braun's contract through the 2031 season.

The school announced the extension Thursday. Financial terms weren't released.

Braun is in his fourth season at Northwestern and carries a 20-19 record into Saturday's game with Colorado. Northwestern went 7-6 and beat Central Michigan in the GameAbove Sports Bowl last season.

Northwestern vice president for athletics and recreation Mark Jackson said in a statement that Braun "is everything that we need in a head coach."

"He recruits young men of high character who embrace our elite academic environment and who compete in the most competitive conference in the country," Jackson said. "David develops our student-athletes at a time when retaining talent has never been harder, and they choose to remain Wildcats when other options appear. He does it with a rare combination of relentless competitiveness and integrity."

Braun arrived at Northwestern as a defensive coordinator on Pat Fitzgerald's staff in January 2023 and was named interim head coach later that year after Fitzgerald was fired amid a team hazing scandal. Fitzgerald later sued the school before reaching a settlement.

Northwestern went 8-5 under Braun in 2023 after going 1-11 a year earlier, a turnaround that helped him get the interim tag removed from his title. After slipping to 4-8 in 2024, Northwestern rebounded to earn bowl eligibility last season.

The Wildcats opened the 2026 season by beating South Dakota State 34-18.

"I am so honored to have the opportunity to lead a storied football program at an institution that demands and expects excellence, instills character, and provides a transformative experience for its student-athletes on and off the field," Braun said in a statement released by the school.

Before coming to Northwestern, Braun was a defensive coordinator at the Championship Subdivision level with North Dakota State, which won two titles during his tenure.

Braun was born in Lake Forest, Illinois, about 20 miles from Northwestern's campus.

title: NFL Week 2 picks & predictions: Patriots face 0-2 crisis
description: Several preseason Super Bowl contenders are looking to avoid 0-2 starts in NFL Week 2.
fullText:
NFL Week 2 can be pivotal for several teams looking to avoid an 0-2 start, including the Houston Texans and New England Patriots.

The first weekend of action delivered memorable games, including the Chicago Bears and Jacksonville Jaguars looking excellent on offense. Meanwhile, several disappointing results came by way of the Denver Broncos, Green Bay Packers and Patriots.

Last week, we put together a strong start to the 2026 season with a 10-5 pick record. We'll look to improve on that as the NFL slate shifts to Week 2.

Let's jump into this week's action with 16 games to choose from on the NFL docket.

MORE: Which NFL game should be nationally televised in Week 2?

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes dives for a touchdown against the Denver Broncos in the first half at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Detroit Lions vs.Buffalo Bills (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video)

Both teams enter Week 2 with 1-0 records, but the Lions certainly benefitted from good fortune against the New Orleans Saints. Detroit certainly struggled to put away the Saints, and Josh Allen and Co. will be tougher.

The Bills enter the second week of the season with a lot of confidence after taking down the Houston Texans. Buffalo's strong offensive output is encouraging after D.J. Moore got into the end zone in his team debut. Pick: Bills 27, Lions 21

Carolina Panthers vs. Atlanta Falcons (1 p.m. ET, FOX)

The entire NFC South enters Week 2 winless, but the good news for Carolina and Atlanta is one team has a good shot at picking up their first win.

The Panthers offense showed they can be dynamic against the Chicago Bears. Bryce Young and Co. will likely carry that form over against the Falcons. Pick: Panthers 30, Falcons 20

New Orleans Saints vs. Baltimore Ravens (1 p.m. ET, CBS)

Baltimore's depleted receiving group is a massive concern against a pesky Saints team. However, do the Ravens need more than Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry to succeed?

New Orleans drops to 0-2 on the season while the Ravens continue to make an argument as the best team in the AFC. Pick: Ravens 21, Saints 17

Minnesota Vikings vs. Chicago Bears (1 p.m. ET, FOX)

The Bears are on a mission to score the most points in NFL history, but the Vikings defense will be a much tougher test than Carolina. Meanwhile, Minnesota will likely need to rely on Carson Wentz for another game as Kyler Murray heals from a concussion.

Chicago has an assortment of offensive weapons, including Rome Odunze and Coltson Loveland. That could prove to be too much for the Vikings to handle. Pick: Bears 27, Vikings 24

New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye throws during the third quarter against the Seattle Seahawks. Mandatory Credit: Steven Bisig-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Cincinnati Bengals vs. Houston Texans (1 p.m. ET, CBS)

The Bengals are looking to go 2-0 after taking down the Buccaneers in Week 1. However, Joe Burrow's status for the game is certainly something to watch.

Meanwhile, the Texans have their own injury concern after Nico Collins left practice on Wednesday. If Collins cannot play, Houston's offense will be far less dynamic. Pick: Bengals 27, Texans 20

Pittsburgh Steelers vs. New England Patriots (1 p.m. ET, CBS)

Maye and New England are facing a major crisis without A.J. Brown for at least the next six weeks. The Patriots' chances of returning to the Super Bowl could be in trouble without another loss in Week 2.

Pittsburgh didn't look impressive at times against Atlanta, but Aaron Rodgers has the benefit of a strong defense. T.J. Watt and the defense can hone in on the Patriots run game with very few pass-catching threats. Pick: Steelers 23, Patriots 17

Green Bay Packers vs. New York Jets (1 p.m. ET, FOX)

Green Bay is in a tough spot after facing ridicule across the league from their Week 1 collapse. Matt LeFleur needs a win and the Jets are typically a get-right game for many teams.

The Packers avoid an 0-2 start and silence the critics for at least one week. Pick: Packers 28, Jets 24

Cleveland Browns vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1 p.m. ET, CBS)

Tampa Bay's strong offense led by Baker Mayfield puts up a win after a tough loss against Joe Burrow and the Bengals. Cleveland might have to strongly consider benching DeShaun Watson if he struggles again in Week 2. Pick: Buccaneers 30, Browns 14

Philadelphia Eagles vs. Tennessee Titans (1 p.m. ET, FOX)

Tennessee looked completely out of sorts against the Jets, and the Eagles boast way more firepower. Jalen Hurts and Co. can look to establish the run a bit more with Saquon Barkley after a slow start.

Meanwhile, the Titans are destined to fall to 0-2 and stir up some early-season troubles for Brian Daboll. Pick: Eagles 34, Titans 21

Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence calls out at the line of scrimmage against the Cleveland Browns. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Jacksonville Jaguars vs. Denver Broncos (4:05 p.m. ET, CBS)

This has the potential to be one of the top games of the weekend, and there's a good chance that Denver falls to 0-2. Jacksonville appears to be an elite offense with Trevor Lawrence leading the way.

Meanwhile, Denver's offense failed to integrate Jaylen Waddle properly against the Chiefs. Sean Payton and Co. have to get back to the drawing board after dropping their second straight game. Pick: Jaguars 28, Broncos 23

Las Vegas Raiders vs. Los Angeles Chargers (4:25 p.m. ET, CBS)

The Chargers need a bounce-back game after losing to the Cardinals, and the Raiders are an ideal candidate. Justin Herbert and the offense looked disjointed, but Las Vegas simply doesn't have the offensive firepower to compete.

Jim Harbaugh and Los Angeles produce in a big way and get to 1-1 before facing Buffalo next week. Pick: Chargers 37, Raiders 17

Seattle Seahawks vs. Arizona Cardinals (4:25 p.m. ET, FOX)

Another week without Sam Darnold means the Seahawks need to rely heavily on their defense. Drew Lock is competent, but it's a tough ask to play mistake-free for two consecutive weeks.

Meanwhile, the Cardinals exceeded expectations after knocking off the Chargers. Jacoby Brissett and Co. looked surprisingly consistent on offense and they can pull off another upset. Pick: Cardinals 24, Seahawks 20

Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott lines up behind center Cooper Beebe during the first quarter against the New York Giants. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Washington Commanders vs. Dallas Cowboys (4:25 p.m. ET, FOX)

Dallas is hoping to get more production out of their top two wideouts in CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. The Giants did a good job of making Dak Prescott uncomfortable in Week 1, but the Commanders defense isn't the same threat.

Meanwhile, Jayden Daniels looked dynamic at times against the Eagles. Washington needs him to get back to his free-flowing play if the Commanders want to get back into the NFC East mix. Pick: Cowboys 34, Commanders 28

Miami Dolphins vs. San Francisco 49ers (4:25 p.m. ET, FOX)

The 49ers have to play the foreseeable future without De'Zhaun Stribling, but San Francisco's offense looks legitimate. Miami's in a world of trouble after falling to the Raiders in Week 1 and failing to protect QB Malik Willis.

San Fran moves to 2-0 and sets up an NFC West matchup with Arizona in Week 3. Pick: 49ers 38, Dolphins 20

Indianapolis Colts vs. Kansas City Chiefs (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC)

Mahomes and Kansas City have a new layer on offense with Kenneth Walker. His dynamic Week 1 showing gives teams yet another problem to worry about as Mahomes returns to form.

Indianapolis knows it can run all day with Jonathan Taylor, but the Colts' passing game may take some time to return to form as Daniel Jones eases back into the system after his Achilles injury. Pick: Chiefs 30, Colts 21

New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart drops back to pass against the Dallas Cowboys during the first quarter at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

New York Giants vs. Los Angeles Rams (8:15 p.m. ET, ABC/ESPN)

The Rams have the brutal task of going from Australia all the way back home to LA to host Week 2. Matthew Stafford and Co. need a victory after the 49ers thoroughly dominated their game in Melbourne.

Meanwhile, the Giants enter this week on a hot streak after beating the Dallas Cowboys. Jaxson Dart and the New York offense are humming, but the Rams are desperate to avoid an 0-2 start. Pick: Rams 28, Giants 23

title: Key a doubt as Swansea face different challenge
description: Vitor Matos says Swansea City must be ready for a different kind of challenge when they bid to maintain their bright Championship start at Lincoln.
fullText:
Vitor Matos says Swansea City must be ready for a different kind of challenge as they bid to continue their bright start to the Championship season at Lincoln City on Saturday (15:00 BST).

Josh Key is a major doubt for the trip to Sincil Bank with the hamstring injury he suffered during last weekend's win over Burnley.

That means a probable start at right-back for Filip Lissah as Swansea prepare for a physical battle against last season's League One champions.

"Lincoln have a really specific way of playing, really competitive in every situation," said Swansea head coach Matos.

"They are quite a direct team with really strong structure to catch a lot of second balls.

"We know which kind of game we're going to face. They are a team with proper physicality, with a proper heart and passion on the pitch, so we need to be ready for that."

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds

Swansea are second in the early Championship table having won four and lost only one of their first seven league games of the season.

They now face a Lincoln side who have been something of a surprise package in the early stages of their first second-tier campaign in 65 years.

Having lost their first two Championship matches, the Imps have put together a five-game league unbeaten run to climb into the play-off places.

"We need to be consistent in our way and be able to play against every type of opponent. That's what we're going to try," Matos added.

"It's going to be a really hard game in a lot of ways, but that's something that we are working on and analysing to do our best."

The loss of Key, Swansea's one out-and-out right-back, would be a blow to Matos given his promising start to the season.

The 26-year-old has featured in all but one of Swansea's league matches this season but has not trained this week.

"We are waiting for another scan to really confirm what's there," Matos said.

Ross Stewart also remains sidelined by a quad injury, with the Scotland striker hoping to return to training during the upcoming international break.

title: Good Morning, Your Toaster Is Compromised
description: Rise & Grind goes live to the software supply chain.
fullText:
The following is a transcript of the 7am hour of Rise & Grind, a nationally syndicated breakfast news programme, first broadcast Thursday 17 September 2026. Transcription by OpenClaw-4.2. Portions of this segment were pre-blurred at the request of the network.

CHIP: Good morning, good morning, welcome back to Rise & Grind, I’m Chip Halloran.

BRIE: And I’m Brie Kensington. Chip, we have to start with the story that has been, and I’m sorry, burning up our inbox all morning.

CHIP: [laughs] She’s been holding that one since four a.m., folks. But it is a serious story. If you own a smart toaster, a connected espresso machine, certain models of pet feeder, you may have woken up on Tuesday to find those devices producing images that we are, frankly, not able to show you before the watershed.

BRIE: We’re going to put some of those on screen now, heavily blurred. What you’re looking at there is a slice of sourdough from a viewer in Nebraska, and burned into that slice is a cartoon fox, wearing sunglasses, in what our legal team have asked me to describe only as “a pose.”

CHIP: The same image, or variations of it, has appeared in latte foam, on the little screens on the front of smart fridges, and in at least one case spelled out in kibble by an automatic pet feeder. One school district in Ohio has pulled its entire cafeteria line. Three manufacturers have issued recalls. And nobody, Brie, seems to be able to tell us who did this or why.

BRIE: Which is why we’ve brought in an expert. Joining us now from her home is Karen Oyelaran, she is an open source security advocate,

BRIE: Researcher, thank you Karen, and Karen, I understand you’ve actually been tracking this particular hack for some time?

KAREN: So it’s not really one hack, it’s the same underlying library being compromised for the third time in about two years. The component is called vulpine-lz4, it’s a compression library written in Rust, twelve stars on GitHub, and it ends up in appliance firmware because a build tool called snekpack vendors it, and most of these manufacturers use snekpack in their over-the-air update pipeline. The original library stopped getting releases when the maintainer left, so snekpack switched to a community fork called foxhole-lz4, and on Tuesday that fork pushed a release with a modified decompression routine. Instead of unpacking the manufacturer’s splash-screen assets it unpacks a hardcoded image buffer, which is the fox. It’s actually the library’s own mascot. Someone has just drawn it in a way the maintainer definitely didn’t.

CHIP: OK so, a lot to unpack there, if you’ll pardon the

CHIP: But let me make sure I’ve got the headline. Vulpine. Is that an individual, is that a group? Where are they based?

KAREN: No, sorry, vulpine just means fox-like. It’s the name of the software. The person who wrote it isn’t the attacker, he’s actually the first victim in a sense, his package keeps getting

BRIE: So there IS a he. There’s a person behind Vulpine.

KAREN: There’s a person who wrote it, yes. Years ago. He’s not involved in this.

CHIP: And who does he work for? Which of the appliance companies?

KAREN: None of them. He wrote it on his own time and published it for free, and then the appliance companies, and honestly thousands of other companies, built it into their products. That’s just how modern software gets made, you pull in hundreds of these small components and most of them are maintained by one or two volunteers.

KAREN: Free like nobody pays him anything. There’s a donate button. I think it’s had about forty dollars through it.

CHIP: Forty dollars total? For software that’s in, you said millions of appliances?

KAREN: Somewhere north of thirty million devices, based on the firmware strings. And that’s just the appliances. It’s also a transitive dependency of cargo, which is the tool that builds most Rust software, so realistically it’s on almost every developer machine in the world as well. This is actually the point I’d really like to get across if I can, because the manufacturers shipping these toasters are

CHIP: And I do want to come back to that Karen, but I think what viewers at home want to know first is, this individual, the Vulpine developer. Where is he now? Have authorities been in contact?

KAREN: He won the EuroMillions in 2024 and moved to Portugal to farm goats. He hasn’t committed to the repository in about two years. Which, again, he’s allowed to do, it’s a hobby project, nobody was paying him to

BRIE: I’m sorry, he walked away? From thirty million devices?

KAREN: He didn’t walk away from thirty million devices, there weren’t thirty million devices when he wrote it. He wrote a compression library, put it online, and other people put it in toasters. He wasn’t consulted about the toasters.

CHIP: Our producers did actually reach out to him overnight, and Brie, I believe we have his statement?

BRIE: We do. I’ll read it in full. “Thank you so much for reaching out. I hear your concerns and I’m committed to doing better, both as a maintainer and as a model. In the meantime, please find below my recipe for a soft-rind chèvre. Warmest regards.” And then there is, in fact, a recipe.

CHIP: So he IS engaging. That’s encouraging, at least.

KAREN: No, that’s not him, that’s an AI auto-responder. He won’t have seen your email, everyone who writes to that address gets the recipe.

BRIE: The recipe looks quite good, actually.

KAREN: It is, I’ve made it. Look, can I just, the reason this keeps happening to this specific library is that it’s underneath billions of dollars of hardware and nobody funds it. There was CVE-2024-YIKES, same package. There was another one in June, CVE-2026-LGTM, same package again, that time it was AI security scanners approving it because the malware asked them nicely. After that one there was a working group set up specifically to look at

CHIP: So there IS a working group. That’s reassuring.

KAREN: It’s never met. It was scheduled into the same slot as the retrospective for the previous incident, which also never met.

KAREN: A calendar invite exists.

BRIE: Karen, I want to bring it back to the images for a second because I think that’s what’s alarming people. We’ve had the network’s standards team look at these and they’ve confirmed that the fox is, and I’m quoting the memo, “depicted as over eighteen and the sunglasses remain on throughout,” so we are able to discuss it. But who drew this? Is this the same person who broke into the software?

KAREN: So the artwork actually predates this attack. It first showed up embedded in the June incident as a decoy, the idea being that automated scanners would hit the image, refuse to describe it, and never reach the actual malware forty lines further down. Which worked, incidentally. This time someone’s just taken that same asset and pointed it at the toast. Honestly the artwork is the least interesting part, the interesting part is that a fork with eleven downloads can push a release on a Tuesday and be on your kitchen counter by Thursday because none of the vendors in between are checking, and none of them are checking because none of them think of this as their code, because they didn’t pay for it, because nobody

CHIP: And the eleven, sorry, you said eleven downloads, earlier you said something about twelve stars, help me out here. Twelve out of what?

KAREN: It’s not out of anything, it’s just twelve people clicked a button that says star.

KAREN: It’s more like a bookmark.

CHIP: Twelve bookmarks. And that’s holding up thirty million toasters.

KAREN: Yes. That is exactly the problem. And the companies selling those thirty million toasters, we’re talking about firms with nine and ten figure revenues, have collectively contributed zero engineering time and about forty dollars to the component they’re all standing on. If even one of them had funded a part-time maintainer, or an audit, or just read the

BRIE: So who’s liable, Karen? If I’m a viewer and my four-year-old has seen this fox on her breakfast, who do I call?

KAREN: I mean, you’d call the manufacturer, they sold you the toaster. But they’ll point at the firmware vendor, and the firmware vendor will point at snekpack, and snekpack will point at a repository whose owner is currently milking a goat. There isn’t a throat to choke here, that’s what I’m trying to

CHIP: But surely someone owns open source. There’s a company behind Linux, isn’t there?

KAREN: There’s a foundation. Several foundations. None of them own vulpine-lz4, it’s one person’s repo. Was one person’s repo.

CHIP: And he’s just allowed to leave it there? Unlocked? For anyone to put foxes in?

KAREN: He put a licence on it that says anyone can use it for anything and he’s not responsible for what happens. Every one of those manufacturers agreed to that licence when they pulled it in. They just didn’t read it, because again, they weren’t paying for it, so nobody thought of it as procurement, so nobody

BRIE: I have to say, Chip, the more I hear about this the more it sounds like these open sources are a bit of a wild west.

CHIP: It really does. Karen, last question because we’re up against the break. Practically speaking. Should people be unplugging their toasters this morning?

KAREN: The manufacturers have all pulled the update, so anything that’s rebooted since yesterday is fine. And I’d just point out that the toast was never dangerous. It’s bread. The dangerous version of this attack is the one you don’t see, where instead of drawing a fox it just reads your wifi credentials, and that version has almost certainly already happened to the same devices via the same library and nobody booked a segment about it because there wasn’t a picture. That’s really what I’d like people to take away, the fox is

CHIP: So the toast is safe to eat.

KAREN: The toast was always safe to eat.

CHIP: There you go. Toast is safe, reboot your appliances, and I’m sure the authorities will get this Vulpine character sorted out. Karen Overland, open source advocate, thank you so much for joining us.

KAREN: It’s Oyelaran, and it’s, no, that’s fine. Thank you for having me.

BRIE: Fascinating stuff. When we come back: he’s fluffy, he’s fearless, and his owners say he simply cannot be contained. Kubernetes the golden retriever is scaling new heights this morning after landing his very first skateboarding sponsorship. That’s next on Rise & Grind. Don’t go anywhere.
