title: Climate change probably weakened glacier behind deadly Nepal floods, study finds
description: Devighat Bazaar, a Nepalese town devastated by last month’s flash flooding.Photograph: Suryams...
fullText:
Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing over a thousand people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.

Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier's collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3.885bn cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.

"Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away," said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.

"When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."

More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.

It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.

The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.

"Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years," the study said. "This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached."

The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.

Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.

Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the "fingerprints of climate change" were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.

Among the study's key findings were:

In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;

July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;

The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;

The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;

A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.

Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.

Clarke said: "We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse."

Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country's foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India "wake up" and accept shared responsibility for the disaster.

Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the "losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities".

He added: "In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that's done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed."

• This article was amended on 17 September 2026. The original version miscalculated a conversion from cubic metres to cubic feet.

title: U.N.-backed experts cite possible U.S. war crimes in Iran strikes
description:
— Human rights experts commissioned by the U.N.’s top human rights body say they have found “reasonable grounds” to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab. They also accuse Iran’s theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people in a report published Thursday.
The report, while not binding, adds to international evidence gathered about crimes in the war in Iran, and could eventually be used in efforts to reach justice in international courts.
fullText:
GENEVA (AP) — Human rights experts commissioned by the U.N.'s top human rights body say they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab. They also accuse Iran's theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people in a report published Thursday.

The report, while not binding, adds to international evidence gathered about crimes in the war in Iran, and could eventually be used in efforts to reach justice in international courts.

The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the U.N.'s top human rights body, which is based in Geneva.

The experts were expected to present their findings on Monday to the council, which is made up of 47 U.N. member countries.

The international fact-finding mission says its findings on U.S. war crimes center on a pair of U.S. airstrikes that killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children.

At the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February, at least one U.S. missile hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, according to an Associated Press investigation. There has been no final accounting of what happened.

Iranian state media have said 168 people were killed in the strike, most of them children.

"Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," a U.N. statement about the team's findings said.

The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request from The Associated Press seeking comment.

In their report, the experts concluded that "the building of the school was the intended point of impact" and the resulting damage wasn't the result of an errant strike or collateral damage from an attack on a compound of Iran's Revolutionary Guard next to the school.

The Trump administration has yet to directly accept responsibility or release the findings of a Pentagon investigation into the school bombing.

The U.N.-backed team based its allegations on two strikes — one involving Tomahawk missiles that hit the "clearly identifiable" school, and another in which Precision Strike Missiles dispersed tungsten pellets over a "clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area" in the southern city of Lamerd, also on Feb. 28.

The U.N.-backed team said 22 civilian men and women were killed. U.S. Central Command has denied responsibility for the strike on Lamerd.

The team found that killings by state security forces in Iran have occurred on a "staggering scale," and civilians faced "gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government."

Iranian security forces carried out "violent repression" over the last two years by firing assault rifles into crowds, beating protesters and arresting healthcare workers, among other things, the team said. Detainees faced torture, and were deprived of legal counsel, leaving their families "in the dark" about their whereabouts, the experts said.

The Tehran government intensified the use of the death penalty, and said more than 70 people – including five women and three boys – remain at "imminent risk of execution," they added.

"The report concluded that many of these gross violations amount to crimes against humanity — including murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians," the statement said.

The experts said the United States and Iran should halt all rights violations and crimes, and provide "full reparations to victims."

The report, built on a "victims-centered approach," was based on interviews with 73 people both inside and outside Iran, along with documentation, satellite imagery, photographic and video material and information from "credible" organizations and experts, the experts wrote.

The ongoing conflict that has driven people from their homes in Iran as well as an internet shutdown and a lack of full cooperation from the two governments partially impeded the team's efforts to get information.

Nearly three dozen requests from the experts for information from Iran's government went unanswered, they said, as have requests in June to the U.S. government for information and meetings with officials.

title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
description:
Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces 
The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.
The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces

The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.

The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.

The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.

“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.

“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”

Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.

Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.

A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.

The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.

Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.

A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.

In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.

The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.

Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.

“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.

“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”

Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.

Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.

“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.

Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.

The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.

Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.

Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.

“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.

Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

title: The Best Home Entertainment Gear of 2026
description: Entertain yourself with the finest stereos, TVs, and entertainment devices this year has to offer.
fullText:
I don't want to be mean—but your streams are too compressed, your pixel count is too low, and your surround sound is not surrounding. It's cool, though, because you can upgrade your outdated TV with a new one, feel actual bass with a new stereo, and otherwise entertain yourself with all manner of home entertainment appliances. The gear listed below is the best of 2026 in different categories.

Samsung's flagship TV is about as good as it's possible for a TV to be. It uses "quantum dot enhanced" OLED technology to deliver the brightest 4K picture of any TV on the market. The colors are HDR10+ certified. The blacks are as black as my soul. The 165Hz refresh rate destroys lag. The S95H offers built-in spatial audio, with room-filling, directional sound, and the design is as excellent as the specs: The screen is matte, and the frame is metallic silver, so it looks like a piece of art, and it's thin enough that you can hang it on the wall like one. It's not cheap, but it's the kind of television that will impress your neighbors.

There are projectors out there with brighter pictures and more features, but the Anker Nebula Cosmos 4K is my pick for best of the year for its balance of quality, portability, and price. A projector like the Epson Pro Cinema LS12000 is nice, but it costs nearly $6,000, and it mounts to the ceiling so you can't use it to show a movie in the backyard or bring it over to your friend Gary's house. The Cosmos is designed for versatility. It automatically focuses and scales its crisp, bright 4K picture on any flat wall in seconds, and it costs less than a grand. It even has a handle for easy carrying.

Soundbars have come a long way in the last decade or so. The best of them, like Sonos' Arc Ultra, dish out sound that rivals multi-speaker set-ups. The Arc Ultra uses "sound motion technology" (that's what they call it, anyway) to push deep bass and clean mids and highs into your eardrums. It can even deliver Dolby Atmos spatial audio, despite being a single speaker.

If you want better sonic separation than you can get with a soundbar, but you don't want to run speaker wire everywhere or deal with a clunky, old-school receiver, the Sony Bravia Theater Quad is the solution. It's four flat, wireless speakers you place around the room or mount to the walls, and a receiver that's about the size of a paperback. Despite their small size, the speakers' front-firing and up-firing drivers bounce sound off the walls and ceilings to create an immersive soundscapes for movies and music.

It seems like every TV, physical media player, and toaster has some kind of smart streaming feature built in, but they are almost always laggy and badly designed. Say "nah" to that noise with Google TV Streamer. The pebble-like set-top streaming box costs less than $200, has a processor that is 22% faster than its predecessor, double the RAM, and an Ethernet port for a solid wired connection. As a bonus, Google TV also acts as a Matter hub to control your smart home. I'm not crazy about the ads and lack of Wi-Fi 6, but until there's a new Apple TV, this is the best streamer on the market.

The Magnetar UDP800 isn't for casual media consumers, but if you're the type who demands picture and sound at the highest possible quality, you'll want to slip your discs into this player from Magnetar: It's a monster. It laughs at the compression of Netflix by reading 4K video at bitrates up to 100 Mbp. It humiliates Spotify with lossless audio in formats like Dolby TrueHD and DTS-HD Master Audio. It is also a true universal player: it plays everything from 4K UHD Blu-rays and standard DVDs to Kodak Picture CDs. Like most niche gear, it's expensive, but being a purist is worth it.

The distinctions between PC, portable, and consoles gaming are blurry these days , so I don't know if the ROG Xbox Ally X20 technically "counts" as a console—but it definitely counts as an awesome piece of home entertainment tech. It's a full-blown Windows 11 PC disguised as a portable gaming system that can hook up to your TV for full console gaming too. The ROG Ally X20 lets you play Xbox Game Pass games and Steam games right out of the box on a portable system, so it's all things to all people.

Rees-Zammit to return to wing for new season
description: Wales and Bristol back Louis Rees-Zammit says he will be a winger who can play full-back this season for club and country.
fullText:
Wales and Bristol back Louis Rees-Zammit said he will be a winger who can play full-back this season for club and country, after spending much of the last campaign in the number 15 shirt.

Rees-Zammit returned to rugby last summer after almost two years away, as he tried to carve out a career in the NFL, and under Bristol boss Pat Lam and Wales head coach Steve Tandy was deployed at full-back consistently from the autumn, rather than his former position on the right wing.

The 25-year-old said he knew last season would likely not be his "best" campaign, after a long period away, and that learning a new position added to the challenge.

"I'm going to be a winger but with the ability to play full-back," he told Rugby Union Weekly.

"I played three-quarters of the season at full-back which I'd never really done before without playing for two years.

"It was hard to settle in but I know that I've played wing for however many years previous, so that's going to help me keep my feet on the ground."

Rees-Zammit feeling 'more comfortable' at full-back

I've not found my feet back in rugby - Rees-Zammit

Of the 22 games Rees-Zammit started last season for club and country, 10 were at 14 while 12 were at 15.

He scored nine tries (seven for Bristol, two for Wales) but only one during 2026 after making the switch - away at Northampton in May when he was back on the wing. In fact, six of the nine tries were scored while playing on the wing.

"I still enjoyed it, I just feel like at 15 you're not as much of a finisher than you are on the wing and that's what I like to be known as," he added.

"Previously I was scoring a lot of tries and I was a good finisher - I'd like to be on the end of that."

Rees-Zammit comes into 2026-27 having had a full summer to prepare although he missed the first block of training with Bristol after spending July with Wales for the Nations' Championship.

The Bears, who have never reached the Prem final, finished sixth in the table last season, missing out on the play-offs by nine points after a drop in form during the spring.

However they finished with 11 wins - the same number as Exeter who were third and reached the final where they lost to Northampton.

"Last year ultimately we fell short of our goal," Rees-Zammit said.

"Although we won the same amount as [third] place, we didn't score enough tries, we didn't have enough bonus points and that's something we're going to try and work on and try and fix for this season."

title: 'Do better kid' - Gaethje rejects Topuria's cheat claim

fullText:
UFC lightweight champion Justin Gaethje has rejected Ilia Topuria's insinuation that he cheated to win their fight at UFC Freedom 250 in June.

Topuria, 29, retired on his stool at the end of the fourth round, losing the title on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington DC.

The Georgian-Spaniard was previously unbeaten but sustained serious injuries to his eye in the defeat as American Gaethje became undisputed champion for the first time.

After a three-month recovery period, Topuria confirmed on X that he has recovered and is ready to return to the octagon, while also taking aim at Gaethje.

"Final medical tests done. I'm back," Topuria posted.

"To all the clowns who've been counting me out this whole time, here I am.

"Next time I'll make sure they check Justin's gloves so he doesn't put anything weird on them. See you soon."

Responding to those allegations, Gaethje, 37, replied: "94 days and the best you could come up with is a lame excuse. As terrible as your last performance. Do better kid."

Topuria reigned as featherweight champion before vacating the title and moving up a division to beat Charles Oliveira for the vacant lightweight belt.

He was making his first defence against interim champion Gaethje.

Gaethje is yet to book his next fight and a rematch between the pair could be on the cards, although Arman Tsarukyan, who faces Mauricio Ruffy, at UFC 331 on Saturday claims UFC president Dana White has promised a title shot to the winner.

title: England batter Donald ready to savour Welsh homecoming
description: Welsh cricketer Aneurin Donald is set to experience one of the most special moments of his life when he opens the batting for England in Cardiff.
fullText:
Welsh cricketer Aneurin Donald is set to experience one of the most special moments of his life when he opens the batting for England in Cardiff on Thursday.

Donald, 29, made his international debut in the crushing 119-run opening T20 victory against Sri Lanka in Southampton on Tuesday, 15 September.

He scored 12 from five balls with captain Harry Brook hitting a brutal unbeaten 114 not out from 49 balls and Jos Buttler scoring 80.

And two days on from becoming the first man who has represented Glamorgan to play for England since Simon Jones in 2005, the explosive batter is looking forward to his Welsh homecoming.

"Getting an international cap on Welsh soil would one of the most special moments in my career," said Donald.

"I've got the opportunity to fly the flag for everyone that's put some time and energy into me, but not just that, the wider Welsh game.

"It's an added responsibility but I'm determined to try and fly the flag."

Donald is a product of Gorseinon cricket club, located in a Swansea suburb, with his parents Andrew and Jocelyn and brother Gafyn among his biggest supporters, alongside Aneurin's partner Heather.

"It would make all the cold, wet winter days in our little one indoor lane shed down there worth it," said Donald.

"It [Gorseinon] is such a special club. Everyone has made sacrifices, from my family through to all my coaches and everywhere I've been before.

"I am sure there'll be a few people coming up and my family have probably bought a stand! There would be a loud corner of people cheering for me."

Donald, who came through the Glamorgan ranks, has been rewarded for his fine form for Derbyshire in the T20 Blast and Trent Rockets in the Hundred.

Following an injury to fellow Welshman Phil Salt, Donald is opening the batting for England - despite the name the team actually represents England and Wales - with Buttler his partner.

"It's surreal and I don't think I've quite come to terms with it," said Donald.

"If you spoke to me a month ago, I'm not sure I would have had this on my radar. It has been been a whirlwind few weeks but a cool place to be.

"Everything you do as a youngster and through your teenage and professional years is building up to this moment."

Donald became the oldest England batting T20 debutant in nine years, with the achievement coming a decade after he captained the under-19 side.

He has had to overcome serious knee injuries suffered in 2019 and 2020 to fulfill his potential.

So did he fear this day would never come?

"Without a doubt," he replied. "I thought this had maybe passed me by.

"I came on to the scene with a lot of opportunity and this [England] was always the aim.

"It is everything you work for but I've had my fair share of ups and downs throughout my career.

"Certainly with my couple of ACL injuries and a few tough years afterwards, an international cap would have been the furthest thing on my list, I was just trying to get back to playing professional sport and hoping my career was not over.

"You think it's probably got away but you never give up. Suddenly here I am."

Donald has established himself as a top-order hitter and excelled in the past couple of seasons.

Captaining Derbyshire this season, he scored 489 runs in 12 matches in the Vitality Blast and hit the most sixes in this year's competition with 37.

That was rewarded with a place in the Trent Rockets squad and he helped them reach the Hundred final, with his strike rate above 200 in both competitions.

Donald also scored 31 from just eight balls for England Lions in a victory against Sri Lanka A at Chelmsford on Friday.

"I've always had an attacking mindset and ability to hit the ball," said Donald.

"In the ever-changing cricket landscape, that's a good place to be.

"The last few years I have doubled down on what am I good at and worked out what my point of difference is.

"I feel as if I've whole-heartedly bought into that and I have to thank Derbyshire for the way they have helped me."

Donald's final achievement was to impress England white-ball coach Brendon McCullum in the Hundred final at Lord's with 38 runs in 19 balls.

"I guess the final tick in the box is being able to get a few runs under pressure on a big stage, while having the England head coach there watching was the ideal setup," said the explosive batter.

"International coaches want to see it with their own eyes and confirm the numbers I've been putting up.

"Hopefully I can play a brand he enjoys and wants to play with England."

Donald is expecting not to be asked to change his approach this week.

"I have been given an opportunity to play a specific role and hopefully bring some wins for England," said Donald.

"That is what's got me to this point, it's a unique way of playing but feel like that's the best for me.

"It's my job to break open games, get ahead of the rate and put on as much pressure as I can earlier, stretching the powerplay.

"I feel I'm right up there with anyone in the country doing that and when you look at all the players around me, it leans even more for me to take on that role.

"When you have got some world-class players sat behind you there's no point in messing around and wasting balls."

Donald certainly does not want to just make up the numbers.

"I want to show I can compete at this level, not just play a small role, but hopefully win games for England," he added.

"On a more holistic level, it is trying to soak it all in.

"I hope I'm going to get more opportunities after this but if this is all I get, it's about enjoying every moment.

"It's about trying not to get caught up in the whirlwind.

"You never know where things end up. It's already been a life-changing few weeks and hopefully that's going to carry on to a few more."

title: London Lions set for NBA test as British basketball bids to step up
description: The 2026-27 Super League Basketball season gets under way on Friday - and could be the most competitive in a generation, according to Newcastle Eagles owner Paul Blake.
fullText:
"I've been involved for 30 years now and it's definitely the most competitive it's been, pretty much in all those 30 years," Newcastle Eagles owner Paul Blake said.

Excitement is building as British men's top-flight basketball prepares for a new season - with champions London Lions gearing up for a prestigious friendly against NBA opposition in Portland Trail Blazers next month.

Before that, though, the third season of the men's Super League Basketball - launched in 2024 after the British Basketball League folded - begins on Friday, as the Lions head to Bristol Flyers.

Last season, the Lions completed a domestic quadruple by winning the SLB Championship, SLB Playoffs, SLB Cup and SLB Trophy - and will be amining for more success when the campaign concludes in May.

This season, there will be 10 teams - up from nine - following the addition of Liverpool Basketball.

SLBW, the women's competition, starts on Saturday, 3 October.

For many SLB clubs, there is optimism going into the new campaign - given some fine recent results and performances.

Manchester Basketball became the first British team to win a qualifying round match in Fiba's Basketball Champions League by beating German side Wurzburg Baskets earlier this week.

Bristol Flyers, meanwhile, will again compete in the European North Basketball League (ENBL), a competition in which Manchester finished runners-up last season.

The Lions are back in the EuroCup for a second straight season, EuroLeague's second-tier European club basketball competition - and are in good spirits after beating EuroLeague outfit Paris Basketball in pre-season earlier this month.

"The league is just getting more and more competitive all the time, so we know we'll be in for a fight again this season," Eagles owner Blake, who is also an SLB director, told BBC Sport.

"The quality of players that are now in the league across the teams top to bottom is, for me, pretty much the highest level it's been. It's extremely competitive."

The Lions want to become one of world basketball's most recognisable clubs.

On 12 October, they will become the first British side to play an NBA team, when they face a friendly in the USA against the Portland Trail Blazers.

"I've wanted to be in the NBA since I was six years old. This is the closest I've ever been," Lions CEO Lenz Balan told BBC Sport.

"It's a really important signal in the basketball world, in the sporting world. This is the ambition. We are absolutely trying to be one of the best clubs in the world."

As well as looking to defend a domestic quadruple, the Lions will hope to improve on last season's EuroCup campaign.

While they did beat eventual runners-up Besiktas Gain in the group stage, they ultimately finished eighth out of 10 teams.

Balan is hopeful that their summer acquisitions, including the loan arrival of 2025-26 EuroLeague winner Keenan Evans, will help the Lions compete in Europe.

"We have ambitions to definitely outperform last year," added Balan.

"It's going to be tough, but these are some of the best players in the world - and I think most people in London and the UK recognise the level of competition that they're playing.

"We're just really focused on executing that vision, getting better and if we keep doing that, I think we're going to get some good results."

Just 15 days after the SLB season tips off, SLBW will do the same.

Cardiff Met Archers host B Braun Sheffield Hatters, the defending championship and play-off winners, in the opening match on Saturday, 3 October.

At Cardiff, four players are salaried while also studying masters degrees at the university.

The rest of the team are made up of players on scholarships, postgraduate and undergraduate students and others that are balancing a career in basketball with full-time work.

"I think there's an opportunity to build something that people genuinely want to watch and follow," Archers head coach Stef Collins, a member of Great Britain's 2012 Olympic squad, told BBC Sport.

"Women's basketball has shown what is possible internationally, particularly with the growth we're seeing in leagues like the WNBA, NCAA College Basketball."

Collins wants SLBW to build on the recent Women's World Cup in Berlin, at which the United States earned a fifth successive title, beating France in the final.

"It was the most-attended World Cup in the modern era with over 230,000 fans in attendance," she said.

"For me, it's also about telling the stories of the players. They're not just basketball players - they're students, they're professionals, they're international athletes, they're role models. If we can showcase that properly, I think there's an exciting future for the Super league."

The WNBA, the independent women's equivalent of North America's NBA, has been among the pioneers in women's sports leagues across the globe.

In 2025, WNBA clips gained more than one billion views on Instagram, making it the most-followed women's sports league on that platform, which Collins feels can help SLBW on its path for development.

"The WNBA is a really good example of what happens when you give women's basketball a platform and make the players and their stories visible," she said.

"But I think there's also a lesson beyond the basketball itself. Women's sport has shown that fans want to connect with the athletes, their personalities and their stories.

"We shouldn't be afraid to market women's basketball differently and allow our players to be themselves."

title: Marchant set on England comeback after Sale arrival
description: Joe Marchant is determined to convince England head coach Steve Borthwick of his Test credentials and convert his famous father-in-law to Sale's cause.
fullText:
Joe Marchant is still reacclimatising.

"I've had a couple of near slip-ups, which I didn't tell any of the lads, where I'm just saying the things you'd say there," he says of training with his new Sale team-mates after three years at Paris-based Stade Francais.

"You can feel the words coming out wrong.

"For a high ball in France, you'd say 'j'ai', meaning 'I have'.

"So I have had to style that out and turn it into 'Joe's'."

Marchant's immersion in French life was swift and total.

He won the most recent of his 26 England caps in the third-place play-off win over Argentina at the 2023 Rugby World Cup. He had been head coach Steve Borthwick's first-choice outside centre throughout the tournament, starting every match bar the pool-stage thrashing of Chile.

But, as England took a lap of honour at Stade de France, Marchant was straight into Top 14 life and the Test exile that accompanies it.

"It was a bit of a strange one, everyone was going home and for me Paris was my new home," the 30-year-old remembers.

"We finished on the Saturday with the boys [England] and I had the team photo with Stade on the Tuesday, so it was just an on-to-the-next mentality."

Alongside the language, Marchant picked up plenty on the pitch during his stint in France. He feels he is a more assertive and communicative player than the one that left Harlequins. The Top 14 pushed him physically as well.

"It is such an intense league," he says. "Every weekend, there's someone who is at least 150kg who always sits out of a five man line-out, and you just have to get ready for that coming every week."

What's coming next in England is less predictable.

Borthwick has asked Marchant, like fellow Sale new boy Courtney Lawes, to prove himself in the Prem before any return to the Test fold.

"Steve and I have had a couple of chats here and there. Nothing crazy, but just a couple of chats," says Marchant.

"That was the main message. Get back on the field and play and see where we go.

"I want to play for England, that's what I want to do. I'm proud to have played for England and I don't want it to be my last time at that World Cup. I want to play again."

Marchant well knows how precious and precarious a Test career can be.

His decision to move to Stade Francais was partly motivated by a chat with Borthwick's predecessor Eddie Jones.

"There were those conversations just before the Autumn Internationals [in 2022] that I wasn't fitting the mould and I wasn't going to play in the World Cup," says Marchant.

"The Stade offer was a good offer that, on the back of the England stuff, seemed like the right thing to do.

"Then three weeks later, Eddie wasn't with England any more."

In the aftermath of Twickenham jeers and a Springbok defeat, Jones had been sacked. Marchant may have signed with Stade for the following season, but Borthwick was still a fan.

"Steve brought me in and we had a really honest chat about who I am as a player, my decision to go abroad and who I am as a person," says Marchant, of his 2023 return to the England fold.

"They were all really positive. From that, we just got pretty aligned. He knew what he wanted from me and how to get it. For me, I just felt like it was really good clarity on what I need to do to get into that England shirt."

Marchant, a rangy runner with an excellent nose for an angle or support line and an impressive aerial game, is an intriguing addition to England's existing midfield options.

Sale, with ambitions to play more expansively after significant squad investment, will hope to provide a platform for both Marchant and Lawes to make their cases a year out from the next Rugby World Cup.

They begin at home to Bristol on Saturday, 26 September. The match away to Newcastle Red Bulls also looms large in Marchant's domestic calendar.

His wife Hollie is the daughter of former Newcastle and England football striker Alan Shearer.

"Yeah, maybe," says Marchant about whether his father-in-law will be down at the Corpacq Stadium to watch him.

"I think the Newcastle game in October will probably be more likely. It's a bit closer to Newcastle.

"Hopefully he's supporting Sale. If he's not, that's not really 'play on'."

Converting Shearer, convincing Borthwick, continuing a Test career - there is plenty to play for for Marchant this season.

title: Former Mercedes design boss Elliott joins Alpine
description: Former Mercedes F1 design boss Mike Elliott joins Alpine as chief technical officer.
fullText:
Former Mercedes Formula 1 design boss Mike Elliott has joined Alpine as chief technical officer.

The 52-year-old will "lead and oversee the technical and engineering functions at the team's factory in Enstone", a statement said.

Elliott's recruitment is the latest step in Alpine's attempt to return to competitiveness after slumping to the back of the field in 2025.

The move marks a return to the team for Elliott, who was principal aerodynamicist there from 2008-12 when the outfit was known as Renault and then Lotus.

Elliott then spent more than a decade at Mercedes through their dominant years with Lewis Hamilton, rising from head of aerodynamics to technical director and then chief technical officer.

An Alpine statement said: "Elliott has a proven track record in the sport, having contributed to an impressive eight constructors' and eight drivers' championships.

"Elliott's arrival at Enstone strengthens the team's technical capabilities as the team looks to build on the improved performances on track and close the gap to the top four teams."

F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco

Verstappen passes 100 amateur karters in 14 laps

Elliott takes his place in the team's engineering structure above executive technical director David Sanchez, who joined in May 2024.

The statement contained no remarks either from executive adviser Flavio Briatore, the team's de facto boss, or managing director Steve Nielsen, their effective team principal.

Elliott will start work at the team's factory in Enstone, Oxfordshire, next week and Briatore and Nielsen will address his hiring publicly at the next race, the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on 24-26 September.

Elliott, whose career in F1 started at McLaren in 2000, left Mercedes under something of a cloud in October 2023, after the design philosophy the team pursued under his leadership for the 'ground-effect' era from 2022-25 proved a failure.

Eliott had taken on the role of technical director from the highly regarded James Allison and led work on the 2022 design, with Allison moving into a more senior role overseeing the wider company as chief technical officer.

Mercedes followed what became known as a 'zero-pod' concept, where the sidepods were pared back to almost nothing as part of an aerodynamic philosophy that aimed to run the car as close to the ground as possible.

In the wind tunnel, it produced prodigious downforce. But the concept was prone to a phenomenon known as 'porpoising', where the airflow stalls under the floor and sets up a high-frequency bouncing motion.

All the teams suffered from this to a degree in early 2022, but Mercedes found it harder than most to get on top of it.

Although Red Bull dominated the 2022 season with a different design concept, which used heavily undercut side pods to channel airflow used to 'seal' the floor, Mercedes stuck to their guns for 2023, convinced the design could be made to work. The decision came against the pleas of Hamilton to change tack.

When the 2023 car was also off the pace, Elliott swapped roles with Allison.

The move was presented by Mercedes as Elliott's own idea, but within six months he had left the company - again, Mercedes said it was Elliott's decision.

The Alpine role is his first in F1 since leaving Mercedes, and it sees him rejoin forces with Briatore and Nielsen, who were both there during Elliott's first spell with the team.

title: Injured Exeter winger Ridl to miss most of season
description: Exeter winger Campbell Ridl is set to miss much of the season after suffering a knee ligament injury.
fullText:
Exeter winger Campbell Ridl is set to miss much of the season after suffering a knee ligament injury.

Ridl had been one of the breakout stars of last season, scoring 17 tries in 24 games including one in Exeter's Prem final loss to Northampton Saints at Twickenham.

The 21-year-old, an England Under-20 player, was hurt in Exeter's opening pre-season game when they lost to Welsh side Scarlets earlier this month.

It is the latest injury blow for Exeter, who will be without Italy lock Andrea Zambonin until November with a shoulder problem.

"It's a pretty significant knee injury, it's ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) with bits and pieces, which looks like cartilage damage as well," Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter told BBC Sport.

"You're talking majority of the season. Good ones can recover pretty quickly and a really fast rehab can be around six months, and then you talk anything up to the nine-month period and beyond if there's more complications.

"I don't think it's going to be a six-month one because of the other bits that have also been damaged in the knee, so unfortunately for Campbell it's going to be relatively long-term this season."

Meet 'the Ostrich' - Exeter's flying wing from out of Africa

Exeter hat-trick winger Ridl a 'huge talent'

Baxter urges Ridl to build on impressive season

Ridl was hurt as he slowed down to get a pass away in Exeter's opening pre-season game, rather than being injured in contact. He tried to play on but was forced to come off the field a few minutes after being hurt.

It is a blow for a player who was seen as one of the brightest prospects in English rugby last season.

He scored back-to-back hat-tricks in Prem Rugby Cup games in February and notched six tries in six Prem games between mid-March and mid-May.

"There's never a good time to have a serious injury," added Baxter.

"But having it at a time when he's played his first decent amount of adult rugby in a proper, tough, long season... now he's got that opportunity to really work on his physical development because obviously the challenges of being ready to play games every weekend are not going to be there.

"There's a good deal of physical development he'll be able to do while he's recovering from injury.

"He's also at university and deep in studies, so you've got to try to look at the positives of these things.

"If it gives him a period of really good development, getting on top of university studies, getting things really in line for next season then you've got to try and look at this as part of the development process he's going to go through over the next five or six years of his career."

title: Field gets first England start in World Cup final rematch with Canada
description: Hooker Bryony Field will make her first start for England as the Red Roses take on Canada, who they beat in last year's World Cup final, in the WXV Global Series
fullText:
Hooker Bryony Field will make her first start for England as the Red Roses take on Canada, who they beat in last year's World Cup final, in the WXV Global Series at Exeter's Sandy Park on Saturday.

Field, who scored a debut try off the bench in the 48-15 win over Australia last weekend, is a product of Huddersfield RFC and was cheered on by a clutch of young girls from the club in the win over the Wallaroos in Salford.

England have a number of absences at hooker with Amy Cokayne injured, Connie Powell recovering from surgery and Lark Atkin-Davies having recently become a mother.

Field starts alongside Maud Muir and Hannah Botterman, who were also part of the replacement front row which helped turn last weekend's game the hosts' way.

There is a new-look half-back combination with Lucy Packer and Zoe Harrison at scrum-half and fly-half respectively, while Jess Breach and Alex Matthews return from injury.

In total, 14 of the squad were also in the matchday 23 for their landmark world-title win the last time the teams met.

"You need rivalries in our sport and our rivalry with Canada is one that has evolved to a great level," said England head coach John Mitchell.

"They are a well-coached team who will bring a different challenge to the one Australia presented. We will be expected to raise our standards."

England have won 34 of their 38 meetings with Canada, including their last 14 in a row. Canada's last victory in the fixture was a 52-17 win in Salt Lake City back in 2016.

After taking on Canada, England will play New Zealand, their closest challengers in the world rankings, at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium on Saturday, 26 September.

Their WXV Global Series campaign then continues on the other side of the Atlantic in October with Tests against Canada in Toronto and Ottawa and a meeting with the United States in New Jersey.

title: Hallgrimsson spoke to players individually about Israel games
description: Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson says he spoke to players in his Republic of Ireland squad individually about the prospect of facing Israel, adding "none of us feel comfortable playing in these games".
fullText:
Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson says he spoke to players in his squad individually about the prospect of facing Israel, and "none of us feel comfortable playing in these games".

Both of the forthcoming Nations League fixtures between the sides are scheduled for neutral venues, with Israel's 'home' game to be played in Hungary on 27 September, and the reverse fixture in Serbia on 4 October.

The Football Association of Ireland confirmed its 'home' tie would be played behind closed doors, while no tickets will be made available for Irish fans for their 'away' game.

After announcing his latest squad, which will also visit Kosovo on 24 September and face Austria at home on 1 October, Hallgrimsson said he had spoken to his players individually "because we shouldn't be doing this in a group talk".

"Obviously we have different opinions, different strength of opinions," he said.

"I think it's best to say, without going into individuals, none of us feel comfortable playing in these games but once we have decided to play them, we all stick together and play as one."

Republic of Ireland to play Israel games as motion passed

Republic of Ireland v Israel to be played at neutral venue

Coleman not included in Republic of Ireland squad

At an extraordinary general meeting in July, delegates backed an FAI motion to proceed with the games amid concerns that boycotting would cause "significant and lasting harm" for the association.

However, the decision has come under increasing pressure, with a 'Stop The Game' campaign launched by Irish Sport for Palestine calling for a boycott.

The campaign has received support from former manager Brian Kerr and ex-player James McClean, and May's friendly against Qatar in Dublin was disrupted when tennis balls thrown onto the pitch.

The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians.

Israel has regularly denied committing genocide or war crimes and has said its actions in Gaza have been justified as a means of self-defence.

Earlier this week, FAI director of football John Martin said the games had created a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone" and insisted players "shouldn't be in a position where they get criticised".

"We want to represent Ireland with the best games and performances that we can. That's the agreement with all of us," added Hallgrimsson.

"Obviously we don't all share the same opinion. That's just human nature."

The Nations League games mark the Republic of Ireland's first competitive action since their World Cup play-off semi-final defeat by the Czech Republic in March.

Since the penalty shootout loss in Prague, they have played four friendlies, beating Grenada and Qatar and drawing with North Macedonia and Canada.

title: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
description: Joanna Wietrzyk has also forfeited her win in the fitness competition after competing last week.
fullText:
An athlete who faced criticism for continuing to compete in a Hyrox event after soiling herself has apologised and said she will retroactively withdraw from the race.

Joanna Wietrzyk offered her "sincere apology" for the incident during the indoor fitness competition in Beijing on Saturday, saying she should have "made a different choice" and exited the event.

Footage of Wietrzyk competing after soiling herself raised concerns about hygiene, leading Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste to apologise for the handling of the situation.

In a statement shared on social media on Thursday, Wietrzyk said: "I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."

Hyrox apologises for allowing race to continue after athlete soils herself

How Hyrox became the latest sporting craze

After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.

Wietrzyk said: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing."

She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness.

"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued.

Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place".

It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".

In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from any future events.

It said on Monday: "There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete."

In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world. The sport debuted in mainland China in late 2024.

Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing last weekend did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including "spitting, nostril clearing, littering, and water abuse".

title: Klopp wants to 'reclaim' flag amid German elections
description: New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election victory.
fullText:
New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election victory.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, falling just short of securing an absolute majority in the regional parliament.

The anti-immigration party also expects strong results in elections on Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Speaking at a news conference to announce his first squad, Klopp stressed he is not a political "expert" but added: "We had an election where some people may have thought it was OK, while others were saying, 'my God, what is happening here?'

"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us.

"I want it so that when someone waves it, no one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."

No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, when the ruling Nazi party carried out the Holocaust.

"I do not want to entrust national pride to the wrong people," said Klopp, who prefers the term "positive patriotism" to "national pride", which he fears can be misunderstood.

The former Liverpool boss added: "I can be proud to be German while also being open-minded and diverse, and kind and friendly."

Klopp also said it was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers but said football can "foster a sense of community, so that people can truly feel the power of sport".

Klopp named 16 uncapped players in a 44-man squad for four upcoming Nations League matches over the space of two weeks.

A group of 24 players will be available against the Netherlands in Amsterdam on 24 September and at home to Greece in Augsburg three days later.

Most of those players will then return to their clubs while the other 20 players will join the group before Germany face Serbia in Munich on 1 October and Greece in Thessaloniki on 4 October.

The first group includes Premier League trio Kai Havertz (Arsenal), Kevin Schade (Brentford) and Anton Stach (Leeds), while Jamal Musiala is selected after twice collapsing during pre-season games for Bayern Munich.

Brentford's Vitaly Janelt has received his first call-up as part of the second group, which also includes Florian Wirtz (Liverpool) and Malick Thiaw (Newcastle).

Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and defender Antonio Rudiger retired from international duty after Germany's second-round exit against Paraguay at this summer's World Cup.

That led to the departure of coach Julian Nagelsmann and the subsequent appointment of Klopp, who had been working as global head of soccer for Red Bull.

title: FA chair demands Infantino release World Cup sell-off documents
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup in a letter sent by Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt.

Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup.

Infantino should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October.

The letter, also sent to Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, makes accusations of failures in governance and a breakdown in culture within the world football governing body.

Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

The proposal was scrapped following widespread opposition from national associations.

Hewitt's letter adds that there should be an independent review of how FFE was conceived, by whom, and how the private investment was put to tender.

Last month, Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at three US courts over the FFE plan, demanded the release of all documents.

Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.

Infantino, 56, will stand for election for a fourth time in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

The Football Association was troubled by the Balogun situation from the outset, and had requested the release of the documents relating to his overturned ban during the World Cup.

Forward Balogun, 25, was allowed to play against Belgium in the last 16 when he would have expected to be serving a one-match suspension.

The striker had been shown a straight red card for a foul on defender Tarik Muharemovic in the 2-0 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina in the last 32.

Fifa then said the automatic one-match ban would be suspended for a year. No reasoning behind the move was provided, beyond citing a rule which allows punishments to be suspended.

The FA, which had sent a letter of support for Infantino's re-election before the Balogun incident, had deep concerns about political intervention.

US President Donald Trump later confirmed he called Infantino asking for Balogun's ban to be reviewed.

Then the FFE proposal, revealed through the media just days after the World Cup final, fractured the game.

Fifa and Infantino were accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation last month.

Many national associations, including those of England, Wales and Scotland, have withdrawn letters of support for Infantino's re-election.

But Infantino still holds a great deal of support around the globe, with the confederations of Africa, South America and Oceania reiterating their backing.

After FFE was cancelled, Infantino called a meeting of the Fifa management board in Rabat, Morocco.

But as yet there has been no contact with the Fifa Council to explain the controversial plan.

That is set to change next month when Infantino must face Hewitt and the other 35 Fifa Council members.

"I told Kevin, I said, 'You might as well vote with the board because it's just not going to matter. ...
fullText:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday evening said he counseled Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh to vote for an interest rate hike because other Fed officials were expected to vote that way anyway.

"I said do what you want because it doesn't matter because he doesn't have the votes," Trump said to reporters as he was traveling in North Carolina to campaign for a Senate candidate.

"I told Kevin, I said, 'You might as well vote with the board because it's just not going to matter. ... The board is very hostile," Trump said. "They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing. They're a bunch of politicians. They are people put on by politicians."

In the same interview with reporters, Trump also suggested that he doesn't expect Warsh to follow his directions, saying he wanted the Fed "to be independent."

The comments came after Federal Reserve officials voted unanimously to increase interest rates by a quarter point for the first time in three years, a move Trump decried on social media hours after the announcement.

Trump's account that he counseled the Fed chair on his vote was not confirmed by Warsh or other evidence. Asked at a news conference about Trump's repeated demands that Fed officials lower rates, Warsh declined to comment.

"I've got nothing for you on the discussion with the president," Warsh said, moving on to say the decision to raise rates was in fulfillment of the Fed's duty to the American people.

The Fed is designed to operate independently of the White House, setting interest rates based on its own best assessment of the economy rather than short-term political pressure. That independence has long been considered a cornerstone of the central bank's credibility - and a source of tension with some presidents, especially Trump, who wants dramatically lower borrowing costs.

Over the years, Trump has made clear he wants a central bank more responsive to his political agenda, pressing for steep rate cuts to ease the cost of financing swelling deficits and exploring options to oust board members appointed by Democrats.

Past administrations have also pressured the central bank, whose independence rests both on federal law and on norms that most recent presidents have been reluctant to test. Top aides to President George H.W. Bush publicly pushed Fed Chair Alan Greenspan to cut rates before the 1992 election. President Joe Biden met with Fed Chair Jerome H. Powell in the White House in May 2022 to show concern about inflation (though Biden stressed that he respected the Fed's independence).

While it's not unusual for presidents to meet with Fed chiefs from time to time, Trump's comments suggested a closer relationship.

A Fed spokesperson did not immediately return a request seeking comment about the conversation between Trump and Warsh.

Warsh, a Fed governor from 2006 to 2011, returned to the central bank in May, after a year in which Trump pressured the Fed in ways without modern precedent. Trump repeatedly criticized Powell, Warsh's predecessor, for refusing to bring rates down; he tried to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook; and he endorsed a Justice Department criminal investigation of Powell. Trump in January chose Warsh to fill the chairman's seat occupied by Powell, who has stayed on at the Fed as a governor. The Justice Department probe was closed.

The Fed's move Wednesday was seen by analysts as bolstering the central bank's credibility after concern that Warsh, who was nominated to the position by Trump, would not do what it took to get inflation under control.

Trump said the Fed board raised interest rates out of hostility toward him.

"They're raising the rates to make Trump do as bad as he can possibly do," the president said. "The problem they have is that we have the greatest economy in history."

title: Bryan Kohberger's family says they support his attempt to challenge conviction
description:
The family of Bryan Kohberger is supporting his efforts to challenge his 2025 conviction, saying in a statement exclusive to ABC News, "Our full support of Bryan’s decision to pursue post-conviction relief does not come from a place of disregard.”
Kohberger, who is currently serving four consecutive life sentences for killing four college students in Idaho, said in his petition that the circumstances of his plea deal are now suspect because, among other things, he was “convinced to falsely confess” to a crime he says he did not commit.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” he said in a statement to the New York Times last month.
Kohberger's family told ABC News that they did not want their support of their son "to compound the unimaginable grief the families have borne so courageously."
"Rather, it comes from our family’s need to see that the complete and unvarnished truth is told.
fullText:
Kohberger is working to undo his guilty plea to the 2022 Idaho murders.

The family of Bryan Kohberger is supporting his efforts to challenge his 2025 conviction, saying in a statement exclusive to ABC News, "Our full support of Bryan’s decision to pursue post-conviction relief does not come from a place of disregard.”

Kohberger, who is currently serving four consecutive life sentences for killing four college students in Idaho, said in his petition that the circumstances of his plea deal are now suspect because, among other things, he was “convinced to falsely confess” to a crime he says he did not commit.

“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” he said in a statement to the New York Times last month.

Kohberger's family told ABC News that they did not want their support of their son "to compound the unimaginable grief the families have borne so courageously."

"Rather, it comes from our family’s need to see that the complete and unvarnished truth is told. Like everyone, we seek answers to all the questions that have been raised, which can only be addressed through a proper trial, as opposed to an improper plea,” the Kohberger family said.

“As a family, we continue to carry the victims, their families, and the entire Moscow community in our hearts and daily prayer,” they added. “We continue to love and support Bryan and we continue to respect the memory of those lost. We seek to find justice and a conclusive resolution through the legal process.”

This month, Bryan Kohberger also requested a new judge to oversee the process, saying comments made by Judge Steven Hippler during his sentencing showed bias. Hippler said he could identify nothing redeeming about Kohberger because his conduct had buried anything "good or intrinsically human," and he called him "the worst of the worst." Kohberger’s motion also asks for his case to be moved back to Latah County, where the killings took place.

A hearing regarding his request for a new judge and location is scheduled for Oct. 15. A hearing to address his motion for post-conviction relief is set for June 17, 2027.

Last year, Kohberger, a former doctoral student in criminal justice, admitted he killed four college students in an off-campus house in Moscow, Idaho, on Nov. 13 2022. In addition to the life sentences, he received 10 years in prison for a burglary charge. The case received international media attention. Kohberger never explained or gave a motive for the killings.

“It is not impossible but not common to have a plea deal returned after a conviction is final,” said Andrea Lewis Hartung, director of Northwestern University’s Center on Wrongful Convictions.

“People accept guilty pleas for all kinds of reasons, not necessarily because they were guilty,” she said. Oftentimes, she said, it is because they “don’t want to take the chance of having such a harsh punishment or were offered lesser charges.”

“A lot of consideration is 'what is the worst case scenario that will happen if you lose.' Whereas if you take a plea, you’ll have a guaranteed result or at least guarantee that you won’t have as harsh of a punishment,” she said.

Under Idaho law, first-degree murder is a crime that can be punished by death or life imprisonment. Prosecutors made it clear early in pre-trial hearings that they intended to seek capital punishment.

Plea deals are often attractive for attorneys to avoid trial. In fact, in any given year, 98% of criminal cases in federal courts end with a plea bargain, according to the American Bar Association. Yet according to the National Registry of Exonerations, about 28% of all exonerated people across the United States since 2014 pled guilty to crimes they did not commit. Likewise, the Innocence Project shows that about 12 percent of known DNA exoneration cases involved an innocent person who pled guilty.

Kohberger’s court-appointed lawyers, led by Coeur d’Alene-based attorney Ann Taylor, spent more than two years challenging evidence during pre-trial hearings. Despite Kohberger’s insistence that he was not guilty throughout the process, his plea deal was announced shortly before his trial was scheduled to begin.

In his new petition, Kohberger claims his lawyers pressured him into the deal with false promises. He said his court-assigned defense team failed to disclose or review exculpatory evidence during discussions and, despite his insistence that he was innocent, he said his attorneys told him that it was legally okay to submit a false guilty plea.

Kohberger “took the plea because he was frightened out of his mind,” Dr. Brent Turvey, a forensic criminologist hired by Kohberger’s legal team to analyze the crime scene, told ABC News. “His lawyers told him it’s okay to lie to the court. His family was used to induce him to take the plea. He didn’t know the strength of his own case.”

Turvey said Kohberger and his family were not given enough knowledge of the case the defense team had built before he pleaded guilty. Turvey explained his report, provided to the defense lawyers, included more evidence that supports Kohberger’s innocence.

Had he had the chance to testify for Kohberger, Turvey said he would have told a jury he was troubled by how investigators documented evidence in the house where the victims were found. He said police did not properly handle the knife sheath after they found it – so much so it should have been ruled inadmissible at trial. Turvey also said, “the hair evidence points to someone else” because FBI analysis “excluded Kohberger.”

He also said video and cell tower data that was used to place Kohberger in the vicinity of the murder scene around the time the killings occurred “has no value or meaning.”

“College students drive around all the time. That’s normal behavior,” Turvey said. “What's really interesting is turning off the cell phone; it is riddled throughout his cell phone behavior. He’ll turn it off and drive around. Why? He’s a college student who doesn’t want to be bothered. You ignore the behavior of real people.”

Ann Taylor did not respond to ABC News' request for comment.

Jason Goldman, one of Kohberger’s new defense attorneys, said plea deals can be thrown out “by bringing evidence to support the notion that you were coerced into accepting a plea through false promises, misrepresentations, or through undue duress.”

“Oftentimes, these very psychological methods could have been employed by an individual’s own counsel, justifying a court’s decision to allow a person to withdraw their plea,” he told ABC News.

“Many individuals take a plea deal even when they are otherwise innocent or believe the evidence against them is weak. Sadly, it becomes less about facts, guilt, or innocence and more about a business decision and being risk-averse,” he said.

Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador released a statement following Kohberger’s petition, saying only that he had sympathy for victim families “who have already endured unimaginable loss” and who now “must face today’s deeply painful news.”

“My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out,” he said.

title: Trump says the EU allowing Canada as associate member could be a 'hostile act'
description:
, Charlotte Van Campenhout and Yves Herman 
   STRASBOURG, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Canada and Europe should ally to protect their markets, democracies and rule of law in a world dominated by the United States and China, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, after an EU ‌proposal to make Canada an "associate member". 
   The Canadian prime minister received warm applause for his speech to the European Parliament, delivered hours after U.S. President Donald ‌Trump threatened trade sanctions in response to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to create a new status for the EU-Canada relationship. 
   Carney did not adopt the term "associate member" used a day earlier ​by von der Leyen, but said he appreciated "the ambition" that her suggestion conveyed.
fullText:
STRASBOURG, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Canada and Europe should ally to protect their markets, democracies and rule of law in a world dominated by the United States and China, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, after an EU ‌proposal to make Canada an "associate member".

The Canadian prime minister received warm applause for his speech to the European Parliament, delivered hours after U.S. President Donald ‌Trump threatened trade sanctions in response to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to create a new status for the EU-Canada relationship.

Carney did not adopt the term "associate member" used a day earlier ​by von der Leyen, but said he appreciated "the ambition" that her suggestion conveyed.

"Europe and Canada are each strong. Europe and Canada are even stronger together," Carney said.

He was not seeking to form a "third bloc" to act as "a great-power rival" to Washington and Beijing "only with better manners," Carney said in a line that drew laughs.

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience, so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, ‌our democracies, our rule of law."

He told reporters after the ⁠speech that it would be up to the EU how it proposed to describe any future relationship, and that the substance of any agreement would be more important than the name given to it.

Trump threatened late on Wednesday to take action against the ⁠EU if it moved forward with von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada an 'associate member' of the bloc.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina, calling the proposal "laughable".

"If it's a good ​intention, ​that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," he added.

The ​European Commission said von der Leyen's proposal — which had yet ‌to be fleshed out and would need to be approved by EU member states to go forward — was not a hostile act.

"As our President (von der Leyen) made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength," said Olof Gill, a European Commission spokesperson.

Asked about Trump's threats, Carney told reporters: "Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally."

title: JD Vance asks voters for 'another chance' as Democrats gain edge ahead of midterms
description:
Vice President JD Vance discussed the White House’s message ahead of the midterm elections on the All-In Podcast, saying, “There’s a lot of good that’s been done, but there’s a lot of work left to do,” adding that the American people should “give us another chance” in November.
